# Area-minimizing submanifolds are not generically smooth

**Authors:** Zhenhua Liu Princeton University Dedicated to Xunjing Wei

## Abstract

We prove that area-minimizing submanifolds are not generically smooth, settling a conjecture of White that asks the generic smoothness of area-minimizing submanifolds. We furthermore establish a lower bound on the Hausdorff dimension of the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds with respect to open sets of Riemannian metrics. The lower bound is $\max\{d-5,d-c\},$ where $d$ denotes the dimension of the submanifold and $c$ denotes the codimension.

## 1. Introduction

The general problem of finding area-minimizing representatives in homology classes is solved by Federer and Fleming ([17]):

Every integral homology class on a compact Riemannian manifold admits an area-minimizing representative.

In other words we can always find a representative of a homology class that has least area among all representatives of the same homology class. The representative in the above result is found in the category of integral currents, which roughly speaking is the closure of the set of algebraic topological polyhedron chains in the Whitney flat topology [17].

Calling the area-minimizing representatives submanifolds was justified due to the following theorem:

An area-minimizing representative of a homology class is a smooth submanifold with integer multiplicities on connected components outside of a singular set of codimension at least $2$ with respect to the submanifold.

Federer first proved the above in [16] when the submanifold is a hypersurface. Almgren [3] proved the above statement in general, and De Lellis, Spadaro, Minter and Skorobogatova ([8, 9, 10, 41, 42, 40]) strengthened the result by showing that the singular set is countably rectifiable. (See also the work of Krummel-Wickramasekera [37, 36, 35].) Thus, we will use interchangebly the terms area-minimizing representatives of homology classes and area-minimizing submanifolds.

The above results on the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds are sharp, as singular sets do appear in very natural settings [15, Section 4]:

Complex algebraic subvarieties, including singular subvarieties, are area-minimizing in the Fubini-Study metric on complex projective spaces.

The presence of singular sets severely restrict the geometric and analytic tools available to obtain meaningful geometric or analytic statements. This raises the natural question of whether one can obtain everywhere smooth area-minimizing submanifolds in generic metrics.

Thom’s classical result [52] shows that there are integral homology classes that topologically cannot be represented by smooth submanifolds. For these homology classes, finding a smooth area-minimizing representative is impossible due to topological obstructions alone. For homology classes with smooth topological representatives, White raised the following question about area-minimizing representatives in [4, Problem 5.16]:

#### Question 1.

”One can also ask whether singularities in a homologically area minimizing cycle in a Riemannian manifold disappear after generic perturbations of the metric.”

Area-minimizing $1$ -dimensional submanifolds are embedded geodesics [16], so White’s conjecture is trivially true in this case. Besides the $1$ -dimensional case, there are only two kinds of progress towards the above question. White solved the above conjecture in the case of $2$ -dimensional submanifolds of arbitrary codimension [56] based on [5, 11, 12, 13]:

In generic metrics, $2$ -dimensional area-minimizing submanifolds of arbitrary codimension are smooth.

On the other hand, the masterful efforts of Hardt-Simon, Smale, Li-Wang, Chodosh-Mantoulidis-Schulze solved the conjecture in the case of low dimensional hypersurfaces [23, 50, 43, 6, 7]:

In generic metrics, area-minimizing hypersurfaces of dimension at most $9$ are smooth.

The above two masterful tour de force results indicate that both the dimension and the codimension of the homology class with respect to the ambient manifold play an important role in determining the generic smoothness of area-minimizing representatives. To this end, we adopt the following notation convention.

#### Definition 1.0.1.

Let integer $d$ denote the dimension of an integral homology class, and integer $c$ denote the codimension of the class with respect to the ambient manifold.

For instance, $d=2$ corresponds to $2$ -dimensional homology classes, and $c=1$ corresponds to hypersurface homology classes. Following this convention, the dimension and codimension of an area-minimizing representative/submanifold will also be denoted by $d$ and $c$ , respectively.

We now state our main results. In sharp contrast to the two masterful results above, the opposite is true in general.

#### Theorem 1.

Area-minimizing submanifolds are not generically smooth, provided one of the following holds,

- • either $d\geq 5$ and $c\geq 3$ ,

- • or $3\leq c\leq d\leq 4$ .

In other words except for the six families of $c=1,$ $c=2,$ $d=1,$ $d=2,$ $d=3<c$ , or $d=4<c$ , area-minimizing submanifolds are not generically smooth.

Our results can be stated more precisely as follows.

#### Definition 1.0.2.

Let $M^{d+c}$ be a compact smooth oriented $(d+c)$ -dimensional manifold and $[\Sigma]\in H_{d}(M,\mathbb{Z})$ be a $d$ -dimensional integral homology class.

For a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ on $M^{d+c}$ , we define $\inf\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,([\Sigma],g)$ to be the lowest possible dimension of singular sets of all area-minimizing submanifolds $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to the metric $g:$

$$ \displaystyle\inf\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,([\Sigma],g)=\inf_{\{T|T\textnormal{ is area-minimizing in }[\Sigma]\textnormal{ in }g\}}\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,T, $$

where ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,T$ denotes the singular set of $T$ , $\dim_{\mathcal{H}}$ is the Hausdorff dimension and we set

$$ \displaystyle\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,T=-1, $$

if $T$ is smooth.

The number $\inf\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,([\Sigma],g)$ is non-negative if and only if every area-minimizing representative of $[\Sigma]$ is singular in ambient metric $g$ .

For homology classes $[\Sigma]$ that do not have smooth topological representatives, no smooth area-minimizing submanifolds exist, regardless of ambient metrics. For a zero homology class, any area-minimizing representative is necessarily zero as $d$ -dimensional integral currents, and consequently never a smooth $d$ -dimensional submanifold. Thus, we only have to focus our attention on the non-zero classes that do have smooth representatives.

#### Theorem 2.

If a $d$ -dimensional non-zero integral homology class $[\Sigma]$ on $M^{d+c}$ admits a smoothly embedded representative with integer multiplicities on its connected components, then there is a non-empty open subset $\Omega_{[\Sigma]}$ of the space of smooth Riemannian metrics on $M^{d+c}$ such that for all $g\in\Omega_{[\Sigma]}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\inf\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,([\Sigma],g)\geq\max\{d-5,d-c\}, $$

provided both $d,c\geq 3.$

Here by an embedded representative with integer multiplicities on its connected components, we mean that

$$ [\Sigma]=\sum_{j=1}^{n}k_{j}[N_{j}], $$

with each $k_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ and $\{N_{1},\dots,N_{n}\}$ a collection of pairwise disjoint smooth submanifolds. The topology we use on the space of metrics is the classical weak $C^{\infty}$ topology [30, 19], which is metrizable [22][30, page 35] and is the same as the Whitney $C^{\infty}$ topology on compact manifolds [30].

In other words there exists an open set $\Omega_{[\Sigma]}$ in the space of smooth Riemannian metrics, such that every area-minimizing integral current in $[\Sigma]$ with respect to an ambient metric $g\in\Omega_{[\Sigma]}$ has a non-empty singular set of Hausdorff dimension at least $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ , provided both $d\geq 3,c\geq 3.$ The statement is not vacuous only when $d\geq 5,c\geq 3$ or $3\leq c\leq d\leq 4,$ thus implying Theorem 1.

Theorem 2 also implies that when $d$ or $(d-c)$ is large, the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds are forced to be large with respect to an open set $\Omega_{[\Sigma]}$ in the space of smooth Riemannian metrics as well.

For the six families $c=1,$ $c=2,$ $d=1,$ $d=2,$ $d=3<c,$ or $d=4<c,$ that are not dealt with in our Theorems 1 and 2, the case of $d=1$ is smooth, as $1$ -dimensional area-minimizing submanifolds are embedded geodesics [16]. The case of surfaces, i.e., $d=2$ , is proven to be generically smooth by White [56]. Since our Theorem 2 includes all dimensions $d\geq 3,$ not considering the the value of $c,$ the theorem is sharp in terms of the dimension $d$ alone. The case of $c=1,$ i.e., hypersurfaces, is widely believed to be generically smooth as well, with the best result obtained by Chodosh-Mantoulidis-Schulze [6, 7]. For the rest of the cases that are not covered by our theorem, all the known examples are generically smooth as well. Thus, we conjecture that Theorems 1 give necessary and sufficient conditions on the dimension and codimension pairs for the generic smoothness of area-minimizing submanifolds:

#### Conjecture 1.

Area-minimizing submanifolds are smooth in generic metrics if and only if $c=1,$ $c=2,$ $d=1,$ $d=2,$ $d=3<c,$ or $d=4<c.$

For a sanity check of the above conjecture, Thom’s result [52] shows that one can find integral homology classes with no smooth representatives if and only if $d\geq 7$ and $c\geq 3.$ Thus, homology classes in the six families $c=1,$ $c=2,$ $d=1,$ $d=2,$ $d=3<c,$ or $d=4<c$ always have smooth topological representatives. Interestingly, by Thom’s classical work [52], persistent singular sets in topological representatives start appearing from $d=7,$ while in our Theorems 1 and 2, persistent singular sets in area-minimizing representatives start appearing from $d=3.$

We also conjecture that the dimension lower bound on the singular sets in Theorem 2 is an upper bound in generic metrics:

#### Conjecture 2.

In generic metrics, area-minimizing submanifolds have a singular set of dimension at most $\max\{d-5,d-c\},$ provided $d\geq 5,c\geq 3,$ or $3\leq c\leq d\leq 4,$ and this upper bound $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ can always be achieved in an open subset of the set of generic metrics.

In other words in generic metrics, $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ is the maximum dimension of singular sets, and this maximum dimension can be achieved quite often.

Theorems 1 and 2 also hold if we replace integral homology with mod $2$ homology or dropping the orientability of $M$ in Definition 1.0.2. We will discuss this in Section 9.

### 1.1. Plan of our proof

We now outline the plan of our proof for Theorems 1 and 2.

Theorem 1 is a direct corollary of Theorem 2, by adding to the conclusion homology classes with no smooth representatives at all due to topological reasons.

From now on, we will focus on proving Theorem 2.

Recall that our goal is to find open subsets of the space of smooth Riemannian metrics in which the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds are of dimension at least $\max\{d-5,d-c\}.$ We adopt the following definition about persistent singular sets.

#### Definition 1.1.1.

We say a subset ${\mathbf{K}}$ of the singular set of an area-minimizing submanifold $T$ in a Riemannian metric $g$ is a persistent singular subset, if there exists an open subset $\Omega_{T}$ containing $g$ of the space of smooth Riemannian metrics, so that for all $h\in\Omega_{T}$

$$ \displaystyle\inf\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\operatorname{Sing}}\,([T],h)\geq\dim_{\mathcal{H}}{\mathbf{K}}. $$

Then our goal is to find an area-minimizing submanifold with persistent singular subsets of dimension $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ in a smooth Riemannian metric.

For simplicity of exposition, assume that $[\Sigma]$ can be represented by a connected smooth submanifold $N.$ The general case in Theorem 2 of $[\Sigma]$ having a representative with several connected components of integer multiplicities needs a slightly modified argument but all the core ideas remain the same.

The topological representative $N$ has no singular set to start with. Thus, to achieve our goal of having persistent singular sets, we must add singular sets manually to alter the topological representative $N$ while achieving the following four features:

- (1) The added singular sets give an altered topological representative that stays in the same homology class $[\Sigma]$ .

- (2) The added singular sets should have dimension $\max\{d-5,d-c\}.$

- (3) We can find a smooth Riemannian metric $h$ , in which the altered topological representative is area-minimizing.

- (4) The added singular sets have persistent singular subsets for the altered representative area-minimizing in $h$ .

Features (1) and (2) are only about the altered topological representative, while in Features (3) and (4) the altered topological representative is area-minimizing in our newly found metric $h.$

Features (1), (2) and (3) are relatively straightforward to achieve. Feature (1) uses a classical construction due to Smale [50], from which Feature (2) follows naturally. Feature (3) uses Zhang’s work on making topological representatives area-minimizing in [58, 59, 57], while Feature (4) is the hardest part and will take the most efforts.

The core of our paper will center around constructing and proving persistent singular sets, i.e., achieving Feature (4). We rely on the following two central facts, the proof of which will take up the majority of our manuscript:

#### Fact 1.1.2.

Orthogonal transverse intersections in immersed area-minimizing submanifolds are persistent singular sets, provided the dimension and codimension of the immersions with respect to the ambient space are both at least $3.$

Frank Morgan hinted the above fact in [48]. In the case of orthogonal transverse intersections of $3$ -dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{6},$ Gary Lawlor proved the above fact for metric perturbations among Euclidean metrics in [38, Section 6.4]. Our proof of the above Fact 1.1.2 is essentially a vastly upgraded version of Lawlor’s proof.

Roughly speaking, Lawlor found a sufficient condition for whether intersection singular sets are persistent, which only starts to work from dimension and codimension at least $3$ . In Euclidean metrics, the sufficient condition reduces to the existence of solutions to an ODE. The key to our proof is finding the right correction factor for the ODE to work in general smooth Riemannian metrics.

The integer $(d-c)$ is the dimension of the intersection set of $d$ -dimensional transverse immersions of codimension $c$ with respect to the ambient space. This explains the factor $(d-c)$ in our lower bound $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ on the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds in Theorem 2.

Another fact we use is the following. Embed $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ into the unit sphere $S^{7}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{8}$ via the Veronese embedding using Laplacian eigenfunctions as coordinates. Define the cone $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ to be the union of all rays starting from the origin of $\mathbb{R}^{8}$ and passing through a point in the Veronese embedding of $\mathbb{CP}^{2}.$ The cone $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ is area-minimizing (Lemma 8.0.5), and the product $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})\times S^{d-5}$ is area-minimizing in the product $\mathbb{R}^{8}\times S^{d-5}$ with the product metric [25, Chapter II, Proposition 7.10], where $S^{d-5}$ is the standard $(d-5)$ -dimensional sphere. Then we have the following.

#### Fact 1.1.3.

The singular set $\{0\}\times S^{d-5}$ of the $d$ -dimensional area-minimizing submanifold $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})\times S^{d-5}$ is a persistent singular set.

To see the ideas behind the above fact, let us think of the simplest case where $d=5,$ i.e., we have two disjoint copies of $\mathbb{R}^{8},$ each copy with an area-minimizing $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})$ inside. Note that topologically $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ as a manifold cannot be the boundary of any $5$ -dimensional manifold [46, page 203]. Thus any reasonable perturbation of the Veronese embedding of $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ will not bound a smooth area-minimizing submanifold. The above Fact 1.1.3 is heuristically due to this non-bounding property of $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ . The analogues of the above Fact 1.1.3 were first noticed by [26].

Note that the singular set in Fact 1.1.3 has dimension $(d-5)$ . This explains the factor $(d-5)$ in our lower bound $\max\{d-5,d-c\}$ on the singular sets of area-minimizing submanifolds in Theorem 2.

With Facts 1.1.2 and 1.1.3 in hand, our plan is to manually introduce orthogonal transverse immersions or $C(\mathbb{CP}^{2})\times S^{d-5}$ into our topological representative of $[\Sigma]$ , while achieving Features 1, 2 and 3. Then Feature 4 is a direct consequence of Facts 1.1.2 and 1.1.3, which finishes the proof.

### 1.2. Overview of the paper

Our paper will be structured as follows. In Section 2, we will give some basic definitions.

In Section 3, we will prepare a topological representative of $[\Sigma]$ . In Section 4, we will alter the topological representative of $[\Sigma]$ to add our desired singular sets, while establishing Features 1 and 2 of our plan. In Section 5, we establish some technical topological lemmas that are needed for Section 6.

In Section 6, we will find a smooth Riemannian metric in which the altered representative produced in Section 4 is area-minimizing, thus achieving Feature 3.

In Section 7, we will prove Fact 1.1.2 in the case of our altered topological representative.

In Section 8, we will prove Fact 1.1.3 in the case of our altered topological representative.

In Section 9, we will finish our proof by wrapping up the conclusions from the previous sections. Then we will give some concluding remarks.

## 2. Basic definitions

We will give some basic definitions in this section. The contents are more or less standard and the experienced reader can skip this section.

### 2.1. Manifolds

As we deal with integral homology in this manuscript, unless otherwise stated, every manifold and submanifold we mention in this manuscript is assumed to be orientable.

In general, the symbol $M$ will be reserved for a $(d+c)$ -dimensional closed ambient manifold and the symbol $[\Sigma]$ will be reserved for a $d$ -dimensional homology class. When we do not mention the ambient manifold explicitly, it is understood that the ambient manifold is $M.$

We will often speak of smooth neighborhoods or smooth open sets, by which we mean an open set with smooth boundary.

We will also make frequent use of transversality [30]. By this we mean that whenever we have a pair of smooth submanifolds of possibly different dimension, we can assume without loss of generality that the pair is transverse to each other and thus intersects along a submanifold.

### 2.2. Riemannian geometry

When a submanifold $N$ is equipped with the induced Riemannian metric, we will use $\mathbf{d}_{N}(p,q)$ to denote the Riemannian distance between points $(p,q)$ on $N$ . And $\mathbf{d}_{M}(p,K)$ will be used to denote the Riemannian distance of $p$ to a closed subset $K$ on $M.$

We will reserve the symbol $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ to denote the Riemannian length of vectors, forms, etc. Whenever we use the symbol $|\cdot|,$ it is understood that we are either taking absolute value or taking the square root of the sum of squares of components in coordinates, which thus are different from $\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert$ on general manifolds.

### 2.3. Smooth functions with controlled zero set

Let $N$ be a smooth orientable Riemannian manifold. Let $K$ be a compact closed subset of $N.$ We need the following lemma.

#### Lemma 2.3.1.

There exists a smooth function $f$ on $N$ such that the zero set of $f$ is $K,$ i.e.,

$$ f^{-1}(0)=K, $$

and $f$ vanishes to infinite order at $K.$

#### Proof.

This is a well-known fact. We only give a sketch here. By Whitney embedding theorem in [55] and the fact that smooth function restricts to smooth function on submanifolds, we reduce to the case of finding a smooth function vanishing with zero set $K$ and infinite order vanishing at $K$ in Euclidean space. By [14, 3.1.13], there exists a good cover of the complement of $K$ with uniform bound on number of intersections. Then for each ball in the covering, we can take a bump function supported on the ball and non-vanishing in the interior of the ball. Now take a sum of these bump functions with small constants in front of each term, so that the sum of $C^{k}$ norm is absolutely convergent for all $k$ . Thus the infinite sum is smooth, and by construction has zero set precisely $K$ . After restricting to an embedding of $N,$ we can adjust the $C^{k}$ norm of the infinite sum by multiplying with small constants. ∎

### 2.4. Unique continuation of minimal submanifolds

In this manuscript, we will frequently use the following classical result:

#### Lemma 2.4.1.

(Strong unique continuation) If two properly embedded $d$ -dimensional minimal submanifolds $F,G$ in a $(d+c)$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold are tangent to each other of infinite order at a point $p\in F\cap G$ , then in a neighborhood of $p$ they coincide.

#### Proof.

This is a classical result, but the author could not find a reference for general codimension in arbitrary ambient metrics. We will only provide a sketch of the proof. Set up a Fermi coordinate [21, Chapter II] chart $(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{d},y_{1},\dots,y_{c})$ centered at $p$ and adapted to $G,$ i.e., $G$ being the $x_{1}x_{2}\dots x_{d}$ -plane in the coordinate chart. By restricting to a small neighborhood of $p,$ we can assume that $F$ can be written as the graph over the $x_{1}\dots x_{d}$ -plane of a smooth function $\overline{F}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{c}$ . Our assumption of $F$ and $G$ tangent to each other of infinite order at $p$ means that $\overline{F}$ vanishes to infinite order at $\{0\}^{d}.$

Write $r=\sqrt{\sum_{j}x_{j}^{2}}.$ Direct calculation shows

$$ \displaystyle|\Delta_{G}\overline{F}|=O\left(|\overline{F}|+r|{\operatorname{d}}\overline{F}|\right). $$

Here $\Delta_{G}$ is the Laplacian on $G.$ Now a classical argument using the monotonicity formula of frequency functions finishes the proof. For precise reference, we can use [34, Theorem 1.8, condition (1.4) with $f=r^{2}$ ] to deduce that $\overline{F}$ vanishes around $p$ , and we are done. Note that [34, Theorem 1.8] says the required condition is [34, Condition (1.3)]. Unfortunately that is a typo in [34], as all the proof in [34] cites [34, Condition (1.4)]. ∎

### 2.5. Definition of area-minimizing.

The right category to discuss area-minimizing representatives is the category of integral currents. We will use Federer’s definitive monograph [14] and Simon’s classical lecture notes [49] as basic references.

For our purposes, the reader can just regard integral currents as integer coefficient chains of simplicial complexes in algebraic topology. Note that integral currents are allowed to have finite area boundaries.

We say an integral current $T$ is area-minimizing, if $T$ has the least area among all integral currents homologous to $T$ :

#### Definition 2.5.1.

A $d$ -dimensional integral current $T$ is area-minimizing if

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}(T)\leq\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V), $$

for all $(d+1)$ -dimensional integral currents $V$ .

Here $\mathbf{M}$ is the mass of the current, which in our context, is just the area of the underlying set with multiplicity included. For instance, $\mathbf{M}(\pm 2S^{1})=2\mathbf{M}(S^{1})=4\pi$ for the unit circle $S^{1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}.$

### 2.6. Definition of singular sets

#### Definition 2.6.1.

We say an integral current $T$ is smooth at a point $p$ in the support of $T$ if there exists an open set $U$ containing $p$ on $M$ , such that $T$ restricted to $U$ equals an integer multiple of a smooth submanifold $N.$ The definitions of regular sets and singular sets of $T$ are as follows:

- • The singular set of $T,$ ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,T,$ is defined as set of points in the support of $T$ where $T$ is not smooth.

- • The regular set of $T,$ $\operatorname{Reg}T$ , is defined as the set of the points in the support of $T$ where $T$ is smooth.

Here support means the underlying set of an integral current. From now on, we will also use the symbol $\operatorname{Supp}T$ to mean the support of $T.$

### 2.7. Multiplicity $1$ integral currents

Many powerful theorems from geometric measure theory deal with a special class of integral currents called multiplicity $1$ currents. We give a formal definition as follows.

#### Definition 2.7.1.

We say an integral current $T$ is of multiplicity $1,$ if $T$ restricted to a neighborhood of each smooth point $p$ equals a smooth submanifold $N$ and the regular set of $T$ is dense in $\operatorname{Supp}T.$

For example, a figure $8$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is a multiplicity $1$ integral current.

### 2.8. Connected sum of multiplicity $1$ integral currents

Many times in this manuscript, we need to use a connected sum to connect a representative of $[\Sigma]$ with multiple components. We give a formal construction as follows.

#### Assumption 2.8.1.

Assume that $T$ and $V$ are two $d$ -dimensional multiplicity $1$ integral currents of dimension $d$ and codimension ${c}$ both at least $\mathbf{2}$ , and both ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}T$ and ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}V$ are non-empty and not equal to each other.

Our goal is to construct a connected sum $T\#V$ .

#### Lemma 2.8.2.

Under Assumptions 2.8.1, there is a multiplicity $1$ integral current $T\#V$ , called the connected sum of $T$ and $V,$ so that

- • ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,(T\#V)={\operatorname{Sing}}\,(T+V)$ .

- • Restricted to a neighborhood of ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,(T\#V),$ the integral current $T\#V$ equals $T+V$ .

- • If $\operatorname{Reg}T$ and $\operatorname{Reg}V$ are both connected, then $\operatorname{Reg}T\#V$ is also connected.

- • $[T\#V]=[T]+[V]$ as homology classes.

For instance, the connected sum of two disjoint embedded tori in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ is a genus $2$ surface. Here the symbol $+$ in $T+V$ means the sum as integral currents.

#### Proof.

In case $T$ and $V$ are disjoint submanifolds, the construction is classical and can be found in [44].

In our case, $T$ and $V$ are general integral currents that may intersect each other and may have large singular sets. However, the idea is similar. We need to remove a $d$ -dimensional ball from $T$ and $V,$ respectively, then use a tube diffeomorphic to $S^{d-1}\times[0,1]$ to connect $T$ to $V.$ The precise construction is as follows.

Take a smooth point $p$ of $T$ , and a smooth point $q$ of $V,$ with $p\not=q.$ Without loss of generality, we can assume that there is an open set $U$ containing both $p$ and $q$ , such that we have a coordinate

$$ (x_{1},\dots,x_{d},y_{1},\dots,y_{c}), $$

on $U$ , with

$$ \displaystyle p=(\overbrace{0,\dots,0}^{d},\overbrace{0,0,\dots,0}^{c}),q=(\overbrace{0,\dots,0}^{d},1,\overbrace{0,\dots,0}^{c-1}) $$

Moreover, the integral current $T$ restricted to $U$ is parameterized by

$$ \displaystyle(x_{1},\dots,x_{d},0,0,\dots,0), $$

with each $x_{j}\in\mathbb{R},$ and the integral current $V$ restricted to $U$ is parameterized by

$$ \displaystyle(-x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{d},1,0,\dots,0), $$

with each $x_{j}\in\mathbb{R}.$ The minus sign is to give opposite orientations in order to carry out the connected sum.

To construct the desired coordinate chart $U$ as above, we need to use transversality. Though in general $T$ and $V$ per se may have complicated singular sets, by Definition 2.7.1 a small perturbation of a smooth curve $\gamma$ from $p$ to $q$ will only meet $T$ and $V$ on their regular sets. By our assumption of codimension $c\geq 2,$ we have $d+1<d+c=\dim M,$ so transversality means that $\gamma$ intersect $T$ and $V$ only at end points, and $\gamma$ is not tangent to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}T$ and ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}V.$ Now take an arbitrary Riemannian metric on $M,$ and extend the unit speed tangent vectors to $\gamma$ to a smooth vector field $X_{\gamma}$ on $M.$ Then apply the flow generated by $X_{\gamma}$ we can bring $p$ and $q$ to the same coordinate neighborhood. It is then straightforward to verify that we can obtain the above coordinate chart $U$ as desired.

Now remove the $d$ -dimensional ball centered at $p$

$$ B_{1}^{d}(0)\times\{0\}\times\{0\}^{c-1}, $$

from $T$ and remove the $d$ -dimensional ball centered at $q$

$$ B_{1}^{d}(0)\times\{1\}\times\{0\}^{c-1}, $$

from $V$ , and glue the tube

$$ \displaystyle S_{1}^{d-1}(0)\times[0,1]\times\{0\}^{c-1}, $$

smoothly onto $T+V$ with the two $d$ -dimensional balls removed, we obtain $T\#V.$ Here by gluing smoothly we mean smoothing the corner introduced by the boundary of the tube. Since our constructions only alter ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}T$ and ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}V,$ we deduce that the first two bullets in Lemma 2.8.2 hold. Since $T$ and $V$ are of dimension at least $2$ , we deduce the third bullet in Lemma 2.8.2. For the last bullet in Lemma 2.8.2, since

$$ \displaystyle S_{1}^{d-1}(0)\times[0,1]\times\{0\}^{c-1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\partial\bigg(B_{1}^{d}(0)\times[0,1]\times\{0\}^{c-1}\bigg)+B_{1}^{d}(0)\times\{0\}\times\{0\}^{c-1}-B_{1}^{d}(0)\times\{1\}\times\{0\}^{c-1}, $$

we deduce that $[T\#V]=[T]+[V]$ . The minus sign in $-B_{1}^{d}(0)\times\{1\}\times\{0\}^{c-1}$ explains the minus sign in parameterization (2.2) of $V$ . ∎

### 2.9. Calibrations

The central object of our manuscript is area-minimizing integral currents. Thus, we must have a way to prove that an integral current is area-minimizing. The way we prove area-minimizing is via calibrations. The notion of calibrations started with the classical paper of Harvey-Lawson [25].

Recall that the comass of a $d$ -dimensional differential form $\phi$ is the maximum of $\phi$ evaluated on simple unit $d$ -vectors in the tangent space to $M$ among all points [14, Section 1.8]. In other words

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{comass}_{g}\phi=\max_{p\in M}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}P\subset T_{p}M\\
\dim P=d\end{subarray}}\phi(P). $$

Here we use the symbol $P$ to denote both a $d$ -dimensional plane $P$ and the unit simple $d$ -vector representing $P.$

For instance, if $\phi$ is a simple form, then the comass of $\phi$ is equal to the maximum Riemannian length of $\phi$ over all points.

For the reader’s convenience, we record some facts about comass.

#### Fact 2.9.1.

Let $g,h$ be positive definite quadratic forms on a finite dimensional vector space, with $\psi$ a constant differential form.

- (1) $\operatorname{comass}_{h}\psi\leq\operatorname{comass}_{g}\psi$ if $h\geq g$ as quadratic forms.

- (2) $\operatorname{comass}_{\lambda^{2}h}\psi=|\lambda|^{-\deg\psi}\operatorname{comass}_{h}\psi$ .

- (3) $\operatorname{comass}_{g}\psi=\operatorname{comass}_{g}\ast\psi$ and $\psi(P)=\operatorname{comass}_{g}(\psi)\iff\ast\psi(\ast P)=\operatorname{comass}_{g}(\ast\psi).$

Here the parameter $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{+}$ , the symbol $\operatorname{comass}_{g}\psi$ means the comass of $\psi$ with respect to $g$ and the symbol $\ast$ is the Hodge star. All the bullets above are direct corollaries of definition of comass. The first two bullets are proved in [57, Lemma 2.1.9, 2.1.20] and the last bullet is proved in [25, Remark at the bottom of p.79]. One can easily adapt Fact 2.9.1 to general Riemannian manifolds.

Now we are ready to give the definition of calibrations.

#### Definition 2.9.2.

(Definition of calibrations)

- • We say a closed $d$ -dimensional Hausdorff measurable $d$ -form $\phi$ on a (possibly open) ambient manifold is a calibration if its comass is at most $1.$

- • We say a $d$ -dimensional integral current $T$ is calibrated by $\phi,$ if $d$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure almost everywhere $\phi$ restricted to the tangent space of $T$ equals the volume form of $T.$

In general, if the calibration form $\phi$ has sufficient regularity, then any integral current $T$ calibrated by $\phi$ will be area-minimizing. The regularity assumption is as follows.

#### Definition 2.9.3.

(Regularity for calibrations to guarantee area-minimizing)

- • We say a degree $d$ closed measurable form $\phi$ has Lipschitz anti-derivatives, if for every point $p$ in the domain of $\phi,$ there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $p$ such that we have $\phi=d\omega$ in $U$ for a Lipschitz $(d-1)$ -form $\omega$ in $U$ . We call $\omega$ a Lipschitz anti-derivative of $\phi$ at $p.$

- • We say a $d$ -form $\phi$ with Lipschitz anti-derivative is almost continuous on an integral current $T,$ if for every point $p$ in the domain of $\phi,$ there is a Lipschitz anti-derivative $\omega$ of $\phi$ at $p,$ such that $\omega$ is continuously differentiable on a subset of $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap\operatorname{domain}\omega$ of full $d$ -dimensional Hausdorff measure.

#### Lemma 2.9.4.

If a $d$ -dimensional integral current $T$ on a compact ambient manifold is calibrated by a degree $d$ calibration form $\phi$ with Lipschitz anti-derivative, then $T$ is area-minimizing (Definition 2.5.1) provided that $\phi$ is almost continuous on $T.$ Furthermore, any integral current homologous to $T$ and having the same area as $T$ must also be calibrated by $\phi.$

#### Proof.

This proof is a straightforward adaptation of [38, Theorem A8] from Euclidean space to general Riemannian manifolds. We will only give a sketch of the argument.

If $\phi$ is smooth, then this is the classical fundamental theorem of calibrated geometry proved by Harvey-Lawson [25, Chapter II, Theorem 4.2]. The proof goes as follows. The condition of comass at most $1$ implies that $R(\phi)\leq\mathbf{M}(R)$ for all $d$ -dimensional integral currents $R.$ Here $R(\phi)$ means integrating $\phi$ on the integral current $R.$ The condition of $T$ calibrated by $\phi$ means that $T(\phi)=\mathbf{M}(T).$ Stokes Theorem and closedness of $\phi$ imply that $T(\phi)=(T+\partial V)(\phi)$ for any $(d+1)$ -dimensional integral current $V.$ Thus, for an integral current $T$ calibrated by $\phi,$ we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}(T)=T(\phi)=(T+\partial V)(\phi)\leq\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V). $$

In other words $T$ is area-minimizing. Furthermore, equality in (2.3) holds if and only if $T+\partial V$ is also calibrated by $\phi.$

When $\phi$ is not smooth, we cannot integrate $\phi$ directly on currents. However, when the ambient space is the Euclidean space we can integrate mollifications $\phi_{\epsilon}$ of $\phi$ on $T.$ The inequality (2.3) becomes

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{M}(T)=(1+O(\epsilon))T(\phi_{\epsilon})=(1+O(\epsilon))(T+\partial V)(\phi_{\epsilon})\leq(1+O(\epsilon))\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V). $$

Taking $\epsilon\to 0$ shows that $\mathbf{M}(T)\leq\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V)$ . This is precisely Lawlor’s proof in [38, Theorem A8]. Again as $\epsilon\to 0,$ we can deduce that $\mathbf{M}(T)=\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V)$ if and only if $T+\partial V$ is also calibrated by $\phi.$

For our proof, we need to work with general manifolds, which does not have the structure of Euclidean spaces. To overcome this, we need to embed our ambient space into Euclidean space to obtain mollifications of $\phi$ . Precisely speaking, isometrically embed the compact ambient manifold into Euclidean space using Nash embedding. Use $\pi$ to denote the nearest distance projection onto the embedded image of the ambient manifold. Then $\pi^{\ast}(\phi)$ is a closed form defined in a tubular neighborhood of the embedded image of the ambient manifold. It is straightforward to check that mollifications of $\pi^{\ast}(\phi)$ can serve the same role as mollifications of $\phi$ in estimates (2.4). Thus, we can still establish an estimate of (2.4). The claim about $\mathbf{M}(T)=\mathbf{M}(T+\partial V)$ implying $T+\partial V$ calibrated by $\phi$ follows directly from this. ∎

## 3. Preparing a representative of $[\Sigma]$

Let us first collect the several assumptions in Theorem 2.

#### Assumption 3.0.1.

Based on Definition 1.0.2, assume both $d,c\geq 3$ and that the non-zero integral homology class $[\Sigma]$ has a smooth representative with integer multiplicities on connected components.

In other words $[\Sigma]$ has an integral current representative as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma=\overbrace{N_{1}+\dots+N_{1}}^{k_{1}}+\overbrace{N_{2}+\dots+N_{2}}^{k_{2}}+\dots+\overbrace{N_{n}+\dots+N_{n}}^{k_{n}}, $$

where $\{N_{1},\dots,N_{n}\}$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint $d$ -dimensional smooth submanifolds and $k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$

However, it will turn out later that the multiplicities $k_{1},\dots,k_{n}$ will prevent us from using many powerful theorems from geometric measure theory. Thus, we need a representative that is of multiplicity $1$ (Definition 2.7.1).

Also, it will become clear later that to make topological representatives area-minimizing, we need the topological representatives to be connected on the regular set.

In this section we will solve these two issues.

### 3.1. Reduction to a multiplicity $1$ current

To destroy the multiplicities of $\Sigma$ in (3.1), first put all the summands in (3.1) into general position:

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma=(N_{1}^{1}+\dots+N_{1}^{k_{1}})+\dots+(N_{n}^{1}+\dots+N_{n}^{k_{n}}). $$

Here each $N_{j}^{k}$ is a perturbation of $N_{j}$ by a generic ambient diffeomorphism into general position. In other words $\Sigma$ is an immersion with normal crossings.

#### Definition 3.1.1.

An immersion with normal crossings is defined to be an immersion that is a stable mapping [19, Definition 1.1].

A mapping is called stable if in the space of mappings there exists an open subset containing the mapping so that all of the mappings in this open subset are equivalent up to an ambient diffeomorphism of the target manifold. Here the topology on the space of mappings is the Whitney $C^{\infty}$ topology [19], which is the same as the metrizable weak topology on compact manifolds [30].

For example, an immersion with transverse intersections is an immersion with normal crossings. Also, the union of $xy$ , $xz$ , and $yz$ -planes in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with coordinate $(x,y,z)$ is an immersion with normal crossings. A detailed exposition of immersions with normal crossings is in the classical work [19, Section III.3]. However, the reader can just regard this notion as a black box, as we only need three consequences of the property of being an immersion with normal crossings.

#### Fact 3.1.2.

Immersed submanifolds $N$ with normal crossings have tubular neighborhoods that deformation retract onto $N$ .

#### Fact 3.1.3.

Immersed submanifolds $N$ with normal crossings are multiplicity $1$ currents.

#### Fact 3.1.4.

There exists a smooth metric $h_{N}$ and a smooth calibration form $\phi_{N}$ on a neighborhood $U(N\cap N)$ of the self-intersection set $N\cap N$ of an immersed submanifold $N$ with normal crossings such that $\phi_{N}$ calibrates $N$ restricted to $U(N\cap N),$ provided the dimension and codimension of $N$ are both at least $3.$

We will prove a much stronger version of Fact 3.1.2 later in the Section 5. Fact 3.1.3 follows directly from definition of immersions with normal crossings in [19, Section III.3].

Fact 3.1.4 is a byproduct of the proof of [58, Theorem 3.20]. [58, Theorem 3.20] states that for embedded submanifolds in general position and linearly independent in real homology, we can find a smooth differential form in a Riemannian metric that calibrates them all at the same time. However, in the proof of [58, Theorem 3.20], a calibration form is first constructed around the intersection set of the embedded submanifolds, and does not use the linear independence condition, which is only used to extend the calibration to be defined everywhere. Thus, the proof of [58, Theorem 3.20] applies to prove Fact 3.1.4.

### 3.2. Connecting the regular set

To make the regular set of $\Sigma$ in (3.2) connected, we need to apply the connected sum of multiplicity $1$ currents defined in Lemma 2.8.2 to $\Sigma$ . In other words we obtain a representative $N$ of $\Sigma$ , where

$$ \displaystyle N=(N_{1}^{1}\#\cdots\#N_{1}^{k_{1}})\#\cdots\#(N_{n}^{1}\#\cdots\#N_{n}^{k_{n}}). $$

By Lemma 2.8.2, $N$ is an immersed connected submanifold with normal crossings, representing the homology class $[\Sigma]$ .

To sum it up, the assumption on $[\Sigma]$ in the statement of Theorem 2 can be reduced to the following assumption.

#### Assumption 3.2.1.

The integral homology class $[\Sigma]$ is represented by a smoothly immersed connected submanifold $N$ with normal crossings (Definition 3.1.1).

## 4. Construction of singular sets

With Assumption 3.2.1 in mind, as outlined in the plan of our proof (Section 1.1), we need to add singular sets manually to the topological representative $N$ of $[\Sigma]$ . The way to do this is to construct a homologically trivial cycle $\sigma_{s}(C)$ on $M$ in Section 4.1 with our desired singular set and using Lemma 2.8.2 to do a connected sum $N\#\sigma_{s}(C).$ This section will be devoted to the construction of the homologically trivial cycle $\sigma_{s}(C).$

### 4.1. The $s$ -th spherical link of a cone $C$

Let $s$ denote a nonnegative integer at most $(d-3)$ that we will set later to be the dimension of the singular set we want to add. Let $V$ be a $(d-s-1)$ -dimensional not necessarily connected closed smooth submanifold of the unit sphere $S^{d-s+c-1}$ of $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ .

#### Definition 4.1.1.

The cone $C(V)$ over $V$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ is defined to be the union of all rays from the origin passing through $V.$

Here by a ray passing through a point $p$ we mean the half line parameterized by $tp$ , with $t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.$

It is straightforward to verify that $C(V)$ is a boundaryless multiplicity $1$ integral current. When $V$ is clear from the context, we will drop the symbol $V$ and write $C$ only. In case $C$ is not a flat subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ , it is straightforward to see that

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Sing}}\,C=\{0\}^{d-s+c}. $$

From now on, we assume that $C$ is not a flat subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ .

#### Definition 4.1.2.

Define the $s$ -th spherical link of $C$ to be

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{s}(C)=(C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1})\cap{S^{d+c}}. $$

The symbol $S^{d+c}$ denotes the $(d+c)$ -dimensional unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}$ and $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$ is embedded naturally in the product $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}\cong\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}.$

It is straightforward to verify that $\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a $d$ -dimensional multiplicity $1$ integral current on the $(d+c)$ -dimensional sphere $S^{d+c}$ .

*Figure 1. Construction of $\sigma^{s}(C)$*

#### Lemma 4.1.3.

There exists a neighborhood $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ of $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ in $S^{d+c}$ diffeomorphic to the product of the unit ball $B_{1}^{d-s+c}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ with $S^{s}$ by a diffeomorphism $\Gamma$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})\overset{\Gamma}{\cong}B_{1}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}, $$

such that $\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ equals

$$ \displaystyle\big(C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\big)\times S^{s}, $$

via $\Gamma.$ Moreover, the singular set of $\sigma^{s}(C)$ is $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ .

Here $S^{s}$ denotes the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$ and we regard $S^{0}$ as two disjoint points. We use the symbol $T|_{K}$ to denote the restriction of an integral current to a set $K.$

#### Proof.

Let us construct explicitly the diffeomorphism $\Gamma$ and its inverse $\Gamma^{-1}.$

Adopt a coordinate system

$$ \displaystyle x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{d-s+c}), $$

on $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ , and a coordinate system

$$ \displaystyle y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{s+1}), $$

on $\mathbb{R}^{s+1}.$ The product structure $\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}\cong\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$ gives a coordinate system $(x,y)$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}.$

Define a map $\Gamma:\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma(x,y)=\bigg(\frac{x}{|y|},\frac{y}{|y|}\bigg). $$

#### Claim 4.1.4.

We claim that $\Gamma$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}$ onto $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$

To prove the above claim, define a smooth map $\Gamma^{\prime}:\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1},$

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{\prime}(x,y)=\bigg(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+|x|^{2}}},\frac{y}{\sqrt{1+|x|^{2}}}\bigg). $$

The map $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is smooth everywhere and we wish to show that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}\right)^{-1}=\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}. $$

Direct calculation shows that the map $\Gamma^{\prime}$ restricted to $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s},$ i.e., where $|y|=1,$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle y\big(\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}(x,y)\big)\not= \displaystyle\,0, \displaystyle\big|\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}(x,y)\big|= \displaystyle\,1, \displaystyle\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}\circ\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}(x,y)= \displaystyle\,(x,y). $$

Here $y\big(\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}(x,y)\big)$ means the $y$ coordinate of $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}(x,y).$ In other words $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ maps $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ to $S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ is a right inverse of $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}.$ Thus $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ must be injective and $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}$ must be surjective onto $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ .

On the other hand, direct calculations also show that $\Gamma$ restricted to $S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\},$ i.e., where $|x|^{2}+|y|^{2}=1,|y|\not=0,$ is a smooth map that satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\Big|y\big(\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}(x,y)\big)\Big|= \displaystyle\,1, \displaystyle\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}\circ\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}(x,y)= \displaystyle\,(x,y). $$

In other words $\Gamma$ maps $S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ is also a left inverse of $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}.$ Thus $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ must be surjective onto $S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}$ and $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}$ must be injective.

To sum it up, both $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ are smooth bijective maps and they are inverse maps of each other. This finishes the proof of Claim 4.1.4.

Now we are ready to find the neighborhood $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ in the statement of Lemma 4.1.3. Since $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ is an orbit of the standard Lie group action

$$ \operatorname{O}(d-s+c)\times\operatorname{O}(s+1), $$

on $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1},$ we deduce that the tubular neighborhoods $U_{r}$ of radius $r$ around $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ in $S^{d+c}$ are also invariant under the action of $O(d-s+c)\times O(s+1)$ as well. Using this, we can calculate that

$$ \displaystyle U_{r}=\{(x,y)\,|\,|x|^{2}+|y|^{2}=1,|x|\leq\sin r,(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}\}. $$

The same calculations as in the proof of Claim 4.1.4 show that $U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}$ is mapped by $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}$ bijectively to $B_{1}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$

#### Definition 4.1.5.

Define

$$ U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})=U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}. $$

To simplify our notations, in this subsubsection we will still use $U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}$ instead of $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}).$

#### Claim 4.1.6.

- • The map $\Gamma|_{S^{d+c}\setminus\{|y|=0\}}$ sends $\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}$ to $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}.$

- • The map $\Gamma^{\prime}|_{\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}$ sends $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ to $\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}.$

To verify the first bullet of Claim 4.1.6, we can parameterize $\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}$ by $(v,y)$ with

$$ \displaystyle v\in C, \displaystyle|v|\leq\sin\frac{\pi}{4}, \displaystyle|v|^{2}+|y|^{2}=1. $$

Thus, on $\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma\big|_{\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}}(v,y)=\bigg(\frac{v}{|y|},\frac{y}{|y|}\bigg)\in C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}, $$

where we have used the fact that $\lambda v\in C$ for any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}.$ This finishes the first bullet of Claim 4.1.6

For the second bullet of Claim 4.1.6, we can parameterize $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ by $(v,y)$ with

$$ \displaystyle v\in C, \displaystyle|v|\leq 1, \displaystyle|y|=1. $$

Thus, on $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{\prime}\big|_{C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}}}(v,y)=\bigg(\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+|v|^{2}}},\frac{y}{\sqrt{1+|v|^{2}}}\bigg) \displaystyle\in \displaystyle(C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1})\cap U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}=\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}}. $$

Again we have used the fact that $\lambda v\in C$ for any $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ . This finishes the second bullet of Claim 4.1.6.

Since $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ are inverses of each other, by Claim 4.1.6 we deduce that $\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ is equal to

$$ \displaystyle C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}, $$

via $\Gamma.$

Now to finish the proof, we need to determine ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C).$ Note that $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$ is invariant under uniform scalings of $\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1},$ i.e., scalar multiples of the identity matrix. Thus, we deduce that the regular set ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}(C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1})$ intersects the unit sphere $S^{d+c}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c+1}$ orthogonally. Orthogonality here gives transversality of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}(C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1})$ with $S^{d+c}$ , which implies that

$$ \displaystyle\big({\operatorname{Reg}\,}(C\times\mathbb{R}^{{s+1}})\big)\cap S^{d+c}\subset{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\sigma^{s}(C). $$

By Definition 2.6.1, this implies that

$$ \displaystyle\big({\operatorname{Sing}}\,(C\times\mathbb{R}^{{s+1}})\big)\cap S^{d+c}\supset{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C). $$

The singular set of $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}$ is $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}.$ Consequently, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)\subset\big(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s+1}\big)\cap S^{d+c}=\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}. $$

Now recall that $\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U_{\frac{\pi}{4}}$ equals $(C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}})\times S^{s}$ via $\Gamma$ . The singular set of $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ is $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$ The inverse image of $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ , i.e., $\Gamma^{\prime}(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ is precisely $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$ We are done. (We emphasize that the two $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ are in different coordinates but are the same set via $\Gamma.$ ) ∎

### 4.2. Adding the singular sets to make an altered representative

Now we are ready to make the altered representative of $[\Sigma]$ with singular sets.

#### Assumption 4.2.1.

Assume $C$ is an area-minimizing cone in $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ calibrated by a smooth calibration form $\phi_{C}$ .

First recall that $[\Sigma]$ can be represented by an immersed connected submanifold $N$ with normal crossings (Assumption 3.2.1).

*Figure 2. Realizing $\sigma^{s}(C)$ on $M$*

Now, let us realize $\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a homologically trivial cycle on $M.$ Pick any point $p$ on $S^{d+c}$ with $p\not\in\operatorname{Supp}\sigma^{s}(C).$ Then $S^{d+c}\setminus\{p\}$ is diffeomorphic to an open $(d+c)$ -dimensional ball. Pick any point $q$ on $M,$ with $q\not\in\operatorname{Supp}N$ , then we can embed $S^{d+c}\setminus\{p\}$ onto an open ball centered at $q$ on $M$ , not intersecting $\operatorname{Supp}N.$ This way we can regard $\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a homologically trivial cycle on $M,$ in the embedding of $S^{d+c}\setminus\{p\}.$

Recall Fact 3.1.4. Now we can use the connected sum defined in Lemma 2.8.2 to construct our desired representative $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ of $[\Sigma]$ with the following properties:

#### Assumption 4.2.2.

$N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a multiplicity $1$ integral current with connected regular set, and

$$ \displaystyle N\#\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U(N\cap N)\cup U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))} \displaystyle=N|_{U(N\cap N)}+\sigma^{s}(C)|_{U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))}, \displaystyle{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right) \displaystyle=(N\cap N)\cup{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)\textnormal{ as a disjoint union}. $$

Here $U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ is just the set $U(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s})$ in Lemma 4.1.3. The change of notation is for coordinate independent expressions.

It may happen that ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\sigma^{s}(C)$ has several connected components. We can still use the connected sum in Lemma 2.8.2 to connect each connected component of ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\sigma^{s}(C)$ to achieve a connected regular set.

## 5. Regular neighborhoods of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$

In the next section, we will need the existence of regular neighborhoods of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ of arbitrarily small radii. A regular neighborhood is a classical concept in piecewise linear topology, and basically is the simplicial version of tubular neighborhoods around simplicial subcomplexes. Heuristically speaking, we need such regular neighborhoods to have a well-controlled local geometry around $N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ which will enable us to make $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ area-minimizing in a smooth metric.

Finding such arbitrarily small radii regular neighborhoods around smooth submanifolds is a classical fact, i.e., just taking tubular neighborhoods of arbitrarily small radii. Unfortunately, $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ has fairly complicated singular set, so we need to go through a more complicated route, by realizing $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a subcomplex of a triangulation and then using the classical regular neighborhood theorem from piecewise linear topology. This section is technical, and the reader can just keep the conclusion of Lemma 5.0.1 below in mind while skipping the proof during the first read through.

We plan to achieve our goal of constructing regular neighborhoods in four steps.

- (1) Prove that $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a Whitney stratified set.

- (2) Whitney stratified sets are triangulable, so $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ can be realized as a subcomplex of a triangulation of $M.$

- (3) By the classical simplicial regular neighborhood theorem, the $n$ -th barycentric subdivision of the triangulation of $M$ with large enough $n$ will yield regular neighborhoods $U_{\epsilon}$ that deformation retract onto $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with $U_{\epsilon}$ arbitrarily close in distance to $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$

- (4) Use Hirsch’s smooth regular neighborhood theorem to upgrade the simplicial regular neighborhoods in the previous step to smooth regular neighborhoods.

Now equip $M$ with an arbitrary ambient metric $h$ . We are ready to state the main lemma in this section.

#### Lemma 5.0.1.

For any $\epsilon>0,$ there exists a smooth open set $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ , such that

- (1) $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ deformation retracts onto $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ by a map $\pi_{\epsilon}$ ,

- (2) $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ is arbitrarily close to $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ i.e., $\displaystyle U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\subset\{p\,|\,\operatorname{dist}_{h}(p,\operatorname{Supp}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))<\epsilon\}.$

- (3) The $d$ -th homology group of $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ is generated by $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ , i.e., (5.1) $\displaystyle H_{d}(U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)),\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)].$

This section will be devoted to proving Lemma 5.0.1. The proof will be carried out in the order of Step (1) and Step (2) together, Step (3) and Step (4) together. Lemma 5.0.1 will be obtained as a direct consequence of the above four steps.

### 5.1. $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a Whitney stratified set and triangulable

Our plan in this subsection is to stratify $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ into disjoint unions of smooth submanifolds of different dimensions, and then prove that the stratification is a Whitney stratification. The Whitney stratification allows us to give a triangulation of $M$ with $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a subcomplex.

An excellent introduction to Whitney’s stratification is available in [53], and the classical reference for triangulation of Whitney stratified sets is [20]. However, since we only use Whitney’s stratification to get a triangulation, the reader can just regard Whitney’s stratification as a black box. Intuitively, it is clear from the constructions alone that $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ can be triangulated.

A Whitney stratification of a closed set $K$ is a finite filtration of closed sets $K_{0}\subset K_{1}\subset K_{2}\subset\dots\subset K_{J}=K,$ such that (the possibly empty) $K_{j}\setminus K_{j-1}$ is a locally finite disjoint union of $j$ -dimensional submanifolds, called $j$ -th strata of $K,$ and each pair of strata satisfies Whitney’s condition (b). Whitney’s condition (b) on an ambient manifold $M$ ([54, Section 1]) is defined as follows:

#### Definition 5.1.1.

For disjoint submanifolds $X,Y$ on $M$ , let a point $y$ be a point in $Y\cap\overline{X}.$ We say $X$ is (b) regular over $Y$ at $y$ , if given sequences $\{x_{i}\}$ on $X$ , $\{y_{i}\}$ on $Y$ , both converging to $y,$ such that the tangent space $T_{x_{i}}X$ converges to a plane $P$ in a coordinate chart, and the unit vector in the direction of $x_{i}$ to $y_{i}$ converges to $v,$ then $v\in P.$

The above definition of Whitney’s stratification is taken from [20, Section 2]. In some literature, authors also require strata in a Whitney stratification to satisfy Whitney’s condition (a), which is long known to be implied by Whitney’s condition (b), e.g., [54, p. 454 last paragraph].

#### 5.1.1. Strata of $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$

First we want to define a filtration

$$ K_{0}\subset K_{1}\subset K_{2}\subset\dots\subset K_{d} $$

for $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ with $K_{j}\setminus K_{j-1}$ a $j$ -dimensional submanifold.

To do this, let us discuss the singularity structure of $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ By Assumption 4.2.2, ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ can be decomposed into the union of $N\cap N,$ the self-intersections set of $N$ , and ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C),$ i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)=(N\cap N)\cup{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C) $$

Recall Lemma 4.1.3, ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ is an embedded standard $s$ -dimensional sphere $S^{s}$ with $s\geq 0.$ Restricted to a neighborhood $U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ around ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ , $\sigma^{s}(C)$ equals $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ via a diffeomorphism $\Gamma.$ Thus, in our construction, we want to make sure ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ is contained in

$$ K_{s}\subset K_{s+1}\subset\dots\subset K_{d} $$

and contributes to only the strata $K_{s}\setminus K_{s-1},$ where we regard $K_{-1}$ as an empty set.

The self-intersection set $N\cap N$ is a bit more complicated. We can decompose $N\cap N$ into disjoint subsets with the same intersection multiplicity, i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle N\cap N=(N\cap N)_{2}\cup(N\cap N)_{3}\cup\dots, $$

where $(N\cap N)_{j}$ denotes the multiplicity $j$ intersection set, i.e. the self intersection points coming from the intersection of $j$ embedded pieces.

In the example of the union of $xy,yz$ and $zx$ -axes planes in $xyz$ -space, the multiplicity $2$ intersection set $(N\cap N)_{2}$ consists of the $x,y$ and $z$ -axis, all minus the origin. The multiplicity $3$ intersection set $(N\cap N)_{3}$ consists of the origin.

Since immersions with normal crossings are stable mappings, it is not hard to show that at any point $p\in N\cap N,$ there is a coordinate system on $M$ centered at $p,$ in which $N\cap N$ becomes the union of at most

$$ \left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1 $$

$d-$ dimensional coordinate axis planes $P_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{k}$ with $k\leq\left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1,$ such that the each pair of planes $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ is transverse for $i\not=j$ , each plane $P_{i}$ is transverse to another pair’s transverse intersection $P_{j}\cap P_{l},$ which is of dimension $(d-c)$ , and so on. Thus, the self-intersection set of multiplicity $j$ , i.e., $(N\cap N)_{j}$ , is an open submanifold of dimension $\left(d-(j-1)c\right),$ i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\dim(N\cap N)_{j}=d-(j-1)c. $$

The above paragraph is taken from [19, Section III.3] and [29, Main Results, p. vii].

Thus, we want to make sure that in our construction $(N\cap N)_{j}$ contributes only to the strata $K_{d-(j-1)c}\setminus K_{d-(j-1)c-1}.$

Now we are ready to describe the filtration $K_{0}\subset\dots\subset K_{d}$ of $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ By the above discussion, we have a decomposition of $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ into disjoint submanifolds of different dimensions as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)={\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\cup{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)\cup(N\cap N)_{2}\cup\dots\cup(N\cap N)_{\left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1}, $$

where each factor in the right hand side is a (possibly empty) smooth submanifold of $M.$ Here we regard $(N\cap N)_{\left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1}$ as an empty set when $N\cap N$ has no points of multiplicity $\left(\left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1\right),$ which is equivalent to $\frac{d}{c}$ being an integer.

If either $s=0$ or $\frac{d}{c}$ is an integer, set $K_{0}={\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)\cup(N\cap N)_{\left\lfloor\frac{d}{c}\right\rfloor+1}.$ Otherwise, set $K_{0}=K_{-1}=\emptyset.$ Suppose we have constructed a $K_{k}.$ If some factor in the right hand side of equation (5.2) has dimension $(k+1)$ , then define $K_{k+1}$ as the union of $K_{k}$ with all the factors in the right hand side of (5.2) that has dimension $(k+1).$ Otherwise, set $K_{k+1}=K_{k}.$ Thus, inductively, we can construct a filtration

$$ \displaystyle K_{0}\subset\dots\subset K_{d} $$

of $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ so that $K_{j}\setminus K_{j-1}$ is a (possibly empty) smooth submanifold of dimension $j.$

#### 5.1.2. Verifying Whitney’s condition (b)

Now we have to verify that each pair of strata satisfy Whitney’s condition (b) (Definition 5.1.1).

First let us decide which strata $K_{j}\setminus K_{j-1}$ can limit to another strata $K_{l}\setminus K_{l-1}$ .

Recall that all strata are the factors of the same dimension in the right hand side of (5.2). Let us consider factor by factor.

Since the regular set ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is dense, ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ can limit to any other strata. Let $\{x_{j}\}$ be a sequence of points in ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ that converges to a point $x.$

If $x\in{\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C),$ then let $\{y_{i}\}$ be a sequence of points in ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ that also converges to $x.$ By Lemma 4.1.3 and Assumption 4.2.2, restricted to a neighborhood of ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ , $\sigma^{s}(C)$ equals $C|_{B_{1}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}\subset B_{1}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}.$ Thus, by choosing a coordinate system on $S^{s},$ we can assume that there is a coordinate chart on $M$ containing $x,$ such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to this chart equals

$$ \displaystyle C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s} $$

Then the $\{y_{j}\}$ lies in $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ , and $\{x_{j}\}$ lies in $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}\setminus(\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s}).$

We claim that line segment $\overrightarrow{x_{i}y_{i}}$ lies entirely on $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s},$ so by definition of tangent space as the set of tangent vectors to curves, $\overrightarrow{x_{i}y_{i}}\in T_{x_{i}}{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ . Thus, Whitney’s condition (b) is satisfied for the strata ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ over ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ . To see this, note that any point $q$ on $\overrightarrow{x_{i}y_{i}}$ equals

$$ \displaystyle q=t\overrightarrow{0x_{i}}+(1-t)\overrightarrow{0y_{i}}, $$

for $t\in[0,1]$ . Since $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ is invariant under uniform scalings, $tx_{i}$ also lies in $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ . Since $C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ is invariant under translations generated by vectors in $\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ , and since $(1-t)y_{i}\in\{0\}^{d-s+c}\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ , we see that $q\in C\times\mathbb{R}^{s}$ as claimed.

If $x\in(N\cap N)_{j},$ adopt a coordinate chart so that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ becomes the union of coordinate planes $P_{1},\dots,P_{j}$ . Let $\{y_{i}\}$ be a sequence in $(N\cap N)_{j}$ with limit $x.$ Then $\overrightarrow{x_{i}y_{i}}$ is always contained in some $P_{l}$ among $P_{1},\dots,P_{j}.$ By definition of tangent space, again we deduce that, $\overrightarrow{x_{i}y_{i}}\in T_{x_{i}}{\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ Thus, Whitney’s condition (b) is satisfied for the strata ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ over $(N\cap N)_{j}$ .

The strata ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ is closed and thus not limiting to any other strata. The strata $(N\cap N)_{j}$ can only limit to $(N\cap N)_{k}$ for $k>j.$ Again, by adopting a coordinate chart where $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ becomes a union of coordinate planes, it is straightforward to verify Whitney’s condition (b) using similar ideas as the previous paragraph.

To sum it up, $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a Whitney’s stratified set.

#### 5.1.3. Realizing $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a subcomplex of a triangulation of $M$

Since we want to use the fact that Whitney’s stratified set can be triangulated, and since we want to realize $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ as a subcomplex of $M,$ we need to include $M$ into the Whitney stratification as well. To do this, set

$$ \operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)=K_{d}=K_{d+1}=\dots=K_{d+c-1},K_{d+c}=M. $$

Since we only added the ambient manifold $M$ to the filtration (5.3), it is straightforward to verify that

$$ \displaystyle K_{0}\subset K_{1}\subset\cdots\subset K_{d+c}, $$

gives a Whitney stratification of $M.$

It is a classical fact that Whitney stratified sets admit triangulations. By [20, Theorem p. 196], $M$ admits a finite triangulation into a simplicial complex, such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a subcomplex. [20, Theorem p. 196] is stated for Thom-Mather stratified sets, of which Whitney’s stratification is a special case as mentioned in [20, Section 1, first paragraph]. To sum it up, we have proven that

#### Consequence 5.1.2.

There is a finite triangulation of $M$ into a simplicial complex, such $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a subcomplex, and ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is a subcomplex of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ .

We have finished Step (1) and (2) of our plan of this section. Now we are ready to deal with the next two steps.

### 5.2. Smooth regular neighborhoods of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ of arbitrarily small radii

In this section we will prove the first two bullets of Lemma 5.0.1, i.e., constructing regular neighborhoods of arbitrarily small radii.

#### 5.2.1. Simplicial regular neighborhoods of arbitrarily small radii

We need the following classical regular neighborhood theorem from piecewise linear topology:

#### Fact 5.2.1.

([32, Theorem 2.11]) The derived neighborhoods $O_{n}$ of a subcomplex $K$ in the $n$ -th barycentric subdivision are regular neighborhoods of $K$ , provided $n\geq 2,$ and each $O_{n}$ deformation retracts onto $K.$

Here the derived neighborhood means the union of all simplices that intersect our subcomplex in the $n$ -th barycentric subdivision, or in simplicial jargon, union of all stars of $K$ . The deformation retract of $O_{n}$ onto $K$ can be constructed by collapsing each simplex intersecting our subcomplex.

We also need another classical fact about diameters of simplices in barycentric subdivisions:

#### Fact 5.2.2.

The diameter of $j$ -dimensional simplices resulting from the $n$ -th barycentric division is at most $\big(\frac{j}{j+1}\big)^{n}$ times the diameter of the original $j$ -dimensional simplex.

This is proved in [27, p. 120].

By Consequence 5.1.2, $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ can be realized as a subcomplex of a finite triangulation of $M.$ By Fact 5.2.1, the $n$ -th derived neighborhood $O_{n}$ of the simplicial realization of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in $M$ deformation retracts onto $N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ By Fact 5.2.2, for any $\epsilon>0,$ there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ large enough, such that

$$ \displaystyle O_{n}\subset\{p\,|\,\operatorname{dist}(p,\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))<\epsilon\}. $$

Though Fact 5.2.2 is stated only for simplices in Euclidean space, we only have finitely many simplices in $M,$ and each simplex in $M$ is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to a simplex in $\mathbb{R}^{d+c}$ . Thus, we can still conclude that the diameter on $M$ of simplices in the $n$ -th barycentric subdivision will converge to $0$ as $n\to\infty.$

#### 5.2.2. Upgrade to smooth regular neighborhoods

We have obtained simplicial regular neighborhoods of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in (5.4). Now we want to upgrade it into a smooth one. This is precisely the conclusion in [31, conlusion (1a’) p. 525]:

#### Fact 5.2.3.

For a simplicial regular neighborhood $L$ of a subcomplex $K,$ and any open set $U$ containing $L,$ there exists a smooth regular neighborhood of $K$ in $U$ that deformation retracts onto $K$ .

Now applying the above fact to

$$ \displaystyle K=N\#\sigma^{s}(C), \displaystyle L=O_{n}, \displaystyle U=\{p|\operatorname{dist}(p,\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))<\epsilon\}, $$

we arrive at a smooth open set $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ that deformation retracts onto $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ by a map $\pi_{\epsilon}$ and

$$ \displaystyle U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))\subset\{p|\operatorname{dist}(p,\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))<\epsilon\}. $$

This finishes the proof of the first two bullets in Lemma 5.0.1.

### 5.3. Homology of $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$

Now we are left to prove the last bullet in Lemma 5.0.1. Since $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ deformation retracts onto $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C),$ to show that $H_{d}(U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)))=\mathbb{Z}[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)],$ it suffices to prove that

$$ \displaystyle H_{d}(\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=\mathbb{Z}[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]. $$

Now we need the following classical constancy theorem from geometric measure theory [47, Theorem 4.9]:

#### Fact 5.3.1.

A $d$ -dimensional integral current $T$ supported on a $d$ -dimensional connected not necessarily closed orientable manifold $N$ equals an integer multiple of $N,$ provided $\partial T$ is supported on $\partial N.$

Let $W$ be a simplicial cycle supported on $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ . Then $W$ induces an integral current supported on $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ . On the connected open manifold ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ , we can use the Fact 5.3.1 to deduce that $W$ restricted to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ is an integer multiple of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right).$ Now that ${\operatorname{Reg}\,}\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ contains all open $d$ -dimensional simplices in $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ , we deduce that $W=k(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ , with $k\in\mathbb{Z}.$ This shows that $H_{d}(\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ is generated by $[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)].$

To finish the proof of Lemma 5.0.1, we need to show that $[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ is not a torsion class on $\operatorname{Supp}N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ Note that there is no $(d+1)$ -dimensional simplex in the triangulation of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C).$ Thus, a $d$ -cycle on $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is a boundary if and only if it equals to $0$ as a cycle. However, $kN\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ for any $k\not=0$ is not equal to $0$ as a cycle. We are done.

### 5.4. Remarks on $U(N\cap N)$ defined in Fact 3.1.4

Recall Consequence 5.1.2 that ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)$ , and thus $N\cap N$ are also a subcomplex of $M.$ The proof of Lemma 5.0.1 also applies to $N\cap N$ . Consequently, without loss of generality, we can assume that

#### Assumption 5.4.1.

$U(N\cap N)$ deformation retracts onto $N\cap N$ .

## 6. Making the altered representative area-minimizing

This section will be devoted to the proof of the following lemma:

#### Lemma 6.0.1.

There is a smooth metric $h$ on $M,$ such that $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ is the unique area-minimizing representative of $[\Sigma]$ with respect to $h$ , provided $2[\Sigma]\not=0.$ When $2[\Sigma]=0,$ $\pm N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ are the unique area-minimizing representatives of $[\Sigma]$ in $h.$ Furthermore, we have

- • In a neighborhood $U_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ of ${\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)$ diffeomorphic to $B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s},$ via the diffeomorphism $\Gamma$ defined in Lemma 4.1.3, the metric $h$ is equal to the pullback under $\Gamma$ of the standard metric on $B_{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s},$ and $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ equals to $C|_{B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{d-s+c}}\times S^{s}$ via $\Gamma.$

Here $B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}$ is the product of a radius ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ ball $B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{d-s+c}$ inside $\mathbb{R}^{d-s+c}$ and the standard $s$ -dimensional sphere $S^{s}$ with ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}>0$ , and

$$ \displaystyle U_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))\overset{\Gamma}{\cong}B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{d-s+c}\times S^{s}. $$

The negative sign $-$ means orientation reversing. Thus, $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ and $-N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ are indeed different as integral currents.

The proof relies on Zhang’s gluing of calibrations in [58, 59, 57]. For the reader’s convenience, we reproduce the entire argument here.

Roughly speaking, the construction of the metric $h$ involves five steps:

- (1) The way we construct $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ provides a Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ and a smooth calibration form $\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ that calibrates $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ restricted to $U(N\cap N)\cup U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)).$ Then we handcraft a Riemannian metric $h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ and a calibration form $\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ that calibrates the regular set of $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ .

- (2) Gluing the metrics $h_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ to $h_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ and the calibrations $\phi_{\operatorname{Reg}\,}$ to $\phi_{\operatorname{Sing}}\,$ , we can construct a smooth metric $h_{\operatorname{glued}}$ and a smooth form $\phi$ calibrating $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ in a smooth regular neighborhood $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ constructed in Lemma 5.0.1.

- (3) Multiplying the metric by a bump function to make $N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ the unique area-minimizing representative of $[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ .

- (4) Making the metric in the complement of $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ very large, so that any area-minimizing integral current $T$ in $[\Sigma]$ will stay in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)).$

- (5) Though homologous objects restricted to subsets of ambient space are not necessarily homologous, the equation (5.1) implies that $[T]=k[N\#\sigma^{s}(C)]$ with $0\not=k\in\mathbb{Z}$ for any integral current cycle $T$ supported in $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))$ . Now use the calibration $\phi$ to deduce that

$$ |k|\mathbf{M}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C))=|kN\#\sigma^{s}(C)(\phi)|=|T(\phi)|\leq\mathbf{M}(T). $$

Then Step (3) forces $T=\pm N\#\sigma^{s}(C)$ provided $T$ is area-minimizing in $[\Sigma].$

After doing some basic preparational works, our proof will be carried in the order of the above five steps.

### 6.1. Preparing the neighborhoods

First of all, we need to prepare the neighborhoods $U_{\epsilon}(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)),U(N\cap N),U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C))$ for our constructions.

#### Definition 6.1.1.

Define

$$ \displaystyle U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)=U(N\cap N)\cup U({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{s}(C)). $$

Note that the union above is a disjoint union.

In order to make space for gluing calibrations in later subsections, we need to retract $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ a bit into its interior. Since $U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)$ is an oriented smooth submanifold with boundary, a neighborhood of its boundary $\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)$ in its interior is diffeomorphic to

$$ \partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times[0,1). $$

We can delete this $\partial\big(U\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right)\big)\times[0,1)$ to obtain a slightly smaller open set $\hat{U}\left({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\left(N\#\sigma^{s}(C)\right)\right).$ In other words we have the following fact
