$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{InjRad}_{X}>{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}, \displaystyle\textnormal{ }\operatorname{InjRad}_{Y}>{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}, \displaystyle\operatorname{FocalRad}_{X,M}>{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}, \displaystyle\textnormal{ }\operatorname{FocalRad}_{Y,M}>{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}, \displaystyle\operatorname{InjRad}L>\frac{\pi}{2}>{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}, \displaystyle X\subset B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(L,X), \displaystyle\textnormal{ }Y\subset B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(L,Y). $$

Here $\operatorname{InjRad}_{X}$ is the injectivity radius of $X$ . It is defined to be the maximum of $\rho$ over all points $p\in X$ such that $\exp^{\perp}_{\{p\},X}$ is injective in $B_{\rho}^{\perp}(p,X)$ wherever it is defined. Also $\operatorname{FocalRad}_{X,M}$ is the focal radius of $X$ inside $M$ , i.e., the maximum of $\rho$ over all points $p\in X$ such that the exponential map $\exp^{\perp}_{X,M}$ restricted to $B_{\rho}^{\perp}(X,M)$ at $p$ is well-defined and injective.

In other words the above assumption roughly says that every point $q\in X$ is of distance at most ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ to $L$ and is in the injective image of the exponential map of the normal bundle of $L$ inside $X.$

### 7.5. Double Fermi coordinates

In this section with Assumption 7.4.4, we will define the double Fermi coordinate chart at a point $p\in L$ adapted to $(L,X,M)$ with radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$ as follows.

#### 7.5.1. Normal coordinates of radius ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ on $L$

For any point $p$ in the Riemannian manifold $L$ , take a normal coordinate chart

$$ \displaystyle l=(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c}). $$

centered at $p$ with radius $r$ . In other words we take an orthonormal frame

$$ \displaystyle\{\ell_{1},\cdots,\ell_{d-c}\} $$

in $\mathbf{T}_{p}L$ , and set the coordinate point $l=(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ to be the injective image of $\sum_{j}l_{j}\ell_{j}$ under the exponential map of $L$ at $p,$ with $\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2}\leq{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{2}$ to utilize Assumption 7.4.4. Our coordinate chart is defined on the ball

$$ \displaystyle B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(p,L). $$

If $d-c=0,$ then skip the above step.

Now define a radial vector field $\partial_{l}$ in the $l$ directions by

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{l}=\frac{l_{j}}{|l|}\partial_{l_{j}}. $$

#### Fact 7.5.1.

In the normal coordinate chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ we have the following:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{l}\perp_{|\cdot|}v \displaystyle\iff\partial_{l}\perp v, \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{l}}\partial_{l} \displaystyle=0,\left\lVert\partial_{l}\right\rVert=|\partial_{l}|=1, \displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{j}l_{j}^{2}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{d}_{L}\Big((l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c}),\{0\}^{d-c}\Big), \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{l_{i}}}\partial_{l_{j}}(p) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\{\partial_{l_{1}},\dots,\partial_{l_{d-c}}\} \displaystyle\textnormal{ is an orthonormal frame at }(0,\dots,0). $$

The symbol $\nabla$ means the Levi-Civita connection with respect to the ambient metric. Here $\partial_{l}\perp_{|\cdot|}v$ at $l$ means that $\partial_{l}$ and $v$ are perpendicular as tangent vectors with respect to the quadratic norm $|\cdot|.$ In other words, if we write $v=v_{j}\partial_{l_{j}}$ with $v\in\mathbf{T}_{(l_{1},\cdots,l_{d-c})}L,$ then we have $\sum_{j}v_{j}l_{j}=0.$ On the other hand $\partial_{l}\perp v$ means $\partial_{l}$ is perpendicular to $v$ with respect to the Riemannian metric.

All of the above facts are classical results about normal coordinates. For instance, the first line is just the Gauss lemma of exponential maps.

#### 7.5.2. First Fermi coordinates of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$

Now take an orthonormal frame

$$ \displaystyle\{e_{1},\dots,e_{c}\} $$

of the normal bundle $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,X)$ at $p$ . Parallel translating the frame $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{c}\}$ along geodesics of $L$ passing through $p,$ we obtain a smooth orthonormal frame $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{c}\}$ of $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,X)$ restricted to $B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(p,L),$ i.e., where the chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ is defined. By construction we have

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{v}e_{j}(p)=0, $$

for any $v$ tangent to $L.$

Now define a Fermi coordinate chart of radius ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ [21, Definition of Fermi coordinates on page 17]

$$ \displaystyle(l,x)=(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c}) $$

adapted to $L$ in chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ with orthonormal frames $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{c}\}$ and $\sum_{j}x_{j}^{2}<\boldsymbol{\rho}^{2}_{\operatorname{product}}.$ In other words the coordinate point $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c})$ is defined by the injective image of the vector $\sum_{j}x_{j}e_{j}$ under the normal bundle exponential map $\exp^{\perp}_{L,X}$ in $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,X)$ at point $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ in normal coordinate chart on $L$ centered at $p.$

If $d-c=0,$ just take a normal coordinate chart $(x_{1},\dots,x_{c})$ in this step.

By Assumption 7.4.4, every point $q$ in $X$ with $\pi_{L,X}(q)$ lying in chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c})$ is contained in our coordinate chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c}).$

Define a radial vector field $\partial_{x}$ along the $x$ -directions by

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{x}=\frac{x_{j}}{|x|}\partial_{x_{j}}. $$

#### Fact 7.5.2.

In the Fermi coordinate chart $(l,x)$ we have the following properties:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{x}\perp_{|\cdot|}v \displaystyle\iff\partial_{x}\perp v, \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{x}}\partial_{x} \displaystyle=0,\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert=|\partial_{x}|=1, \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{x_{j}}}\partial_{x_{i}}(p) \displaystyle=\nabla_{\partial_{x_{j}}}\partial_{l_{i}}(p)=\nabla_{\partial_{l_{i}}}\partial_{x_{j}}(p)=0, \displaystyle\pi_{L,X}(l,x) \displaystyle=(l,0), \displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{j}x_{j}^{2}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{d}_{X}\big((l,x),(l,0)\big), \displaystyle\{\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,\partial_{x_{d-c}}\} \displaystyle\textnormal{ is an orthonormal frame on }\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,X). $$

The proof of the above fact is a straightforward generalization of Fact 7.5.1 about normal coordinates, and can be found in [21, Section 2].

Fact 7.5.1 holds in chart $(l,x)$ when restricted to $\{|x|=0\}.$

#### 7.5.3. Double Fermi coordinate charts of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$

Now let $\{f_{1},\dots,f_{c}\}$ be an orthonormal frame of $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(X,M)$ at point $p.$ Again, we can parallel translate $\{f_{1},\dots,f_{c}\}$ along geodesics of $X$ passing through $p$ to obtain a smooth frame of $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(X,M)$ on chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c})$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{e}f_{j}(p)=0, $$

whenever $e$ is tangent to $X$ . Then define a Fermi coordinate chart with radius ${{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}$ :

$$ \displaystyle(l,x,z)=(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c},z_{1},\dots,z_{c}), $$

adapted to $X$ with chart $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c})$ and frames $\{f_{1},\dots,f_{c}\}$ of $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(X,M)$ with $\sum_{j}z_{j}^{2}\leq{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}^{2}.$ Any point $q$ in $B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(X,M)$ with $\pi_{X,M}(q)$ lying in chart $(l_{1},\cdots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\cdots,x_{c})$ is contained in our chart $(l,x,z)$

#### Definition 7.5.3.

We call the coordinate system $(l_{1},\dots,l_{d-c},x_{1},\dots,x_{c},z_{1},\dots,z_{c})$ the double Fermi coordinate chart of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$ adapted to $(L,X,M).$

Now define a radial vector field $\partial_{z}$ along the $z$ -directions by

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{z}=\frac{z_{i}}{|z|}\partial_{z_{i}}. $$

#### Fact 7.5.4.

In the double Fermi coordinate $(l,x,z)$ we have the following properties

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{z}\perp_{|\cdot|}v \displaystyle\iff\partial_{z}\perp v, \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{z}}\partial_{z} \displaystyle=0,\left\lVert\partial_{z}\right\rVert=|\partial_{z}|=1, \displaystyle\nabla_{\partial_{z_{i}}}\partial_{z_{j}}(p)=\nabla_{\partial_{l_{i}}}\partial_{z_{j}}(p) \displaystyle=\nabla_{\partial_{z_{j}}}\partial_{l_{i}}(p)=\nabla_{\partial_{x_{i}}}\partial_{z_{j}}(p)=\nabla_{\partial_{z_{j}}}\partial_{x_{i}}(p)=0, \displaystyle\pi_{X,M}(l,x,z) \displaystyle=(l,x,0), \displaystyle\sqrt{\sum_{j}z_{j}^{2}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{d}_{M}\big((l,x,z),(l,x,0)\big), \displaystyle\{\partial_{z_{1}},\dots,\partial_{z_{d-c}}\} \displaystyle\textnormal{ is an orthonormal frame on }\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(X,M). $$

Again the proof of the above fact is straightforward and the reader can refer to [21, Chapter 2].

Fact 7.5.1 holds in chart $(l,x,z)$ when we restrict to $\{|x|=|z|=0\}.$ Fact 7.5.2 holds in chart $(l,x,z)$ when we restrict to $\{|z|=0\}.$

### 7.6. Geometric dependence of the double Fermi coordinate chart

At first sight, it may seem that the double Fermi coordinate chart centered at $p$ defined in Definition 7.5.3 depends on a lot of arbitrary choices. However, it turns out the double Fermi coordinate chart is really intrinsically defined up to orthogonal transformations:

#### Fact 7.6.1.

The double Fermi coordinate chart defined in Definition 7.5.3 is unique up to an

$$ \operatorname{O}(d-c)\times\operatorname{O}(c)\times\operatorname{O}(c) $$

matrix multiplication in coordinate.

#### Proof.

By construction, our construction of double Fermi coordinate chart only depends on the choice of orthonormal frames $\{\ell_{1},\cdots,\ell_{d-c}\}$ of $\mathbf{T}_{p}L$ , $\{e_{1},\dots,e_{c}\}$ of $\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,X)$ and $\{f_{1},\dots,f_{c}\}$ of $\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(X,M)$ . All choices of orthonormal frames is equivalent up to an $\operatorname{O}(d-c)\times\operatorname{O}(c)\times\operatorname{O}(c)$ action and by definition of the double Fermi coordinate chart. This $\operatorname{O}(d-c)\times\operatorname{O}(c)\times\operatorname{O}(c)$ action extends to all points of our coordinates. ∎

An immediate corollary of the above fact is that

#### Fact 7.6.2.

The coordinate lengths $|l|,|x|,|z|,$ the vector fields $\partial_{l},\partial_{x},\partial_{z}$ , and all ambient metric inner products among coordinate vector fields and the length of the following multivectors and the length of their wedge products

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}, \displaystyle\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}, \displaystyle\partial_{z_{1}}\wedge\cdots\wedge\partial_{z_{c}}, $$

all depend geometrically (Definition 7.2.1) on $L,X,M$ and the ambient metric.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that

$$ \displaystyle U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)) $$

is contained in the open cover of double Fermi coordinate charts of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$ centered at $p$ with $p$ ranging over all points in $L.$ Since $U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ has compact closure, we can take a finite subcover.

#### Assumption 7.6.3.

There exists a finite subset $\mathbf{F}\subset L$ such that the union of double Fermi coordinate charts of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$ centered at points $p\in\mathbf{F}$ covers $U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{2}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ .

Form now on when we mention a double Fermi coordinate chart, we always mean a double Fermi coordinate chart of radius $({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})$ centered at a point $p\in\mathbf{F}.$

### 7.7. Angled wedges and retractions

#### Definition 7.7.1.

With Assumption 7.4.4, we define the radius $\rho$ , angle $\theta$ , wedge neighborhood of $X$ with vertex $L$ to be

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)=\left\{q\in B_{\rho}(X,M)\bigg|\frac{\mathbf{d}_{M}(q,\pi_{X,M}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X,M}(q),\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(q))}\leq\tan\theta\right\}, $$

provided $0<\rho<{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}.$

By Facts 7.5.1, 7.5.2, and 7.5.4, the geometric meaning of $W_{(\theta,r)}(X,L)$ is that when restricted to the double Fermi coordinate charts $(l,x,z)$ in Definition 7.5.3, we have

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)=\left\{(l,x,z)\bigg|\frac{|z|}{|x|}\leq\tan\theta\right\}. $$

The reader should consult Figure 6 and (7.5) for intuition.

With Assumption 7.4.4, define Lawlor’s retraction $\Pi_{X,L}$ as follows.

#### Definition 7.7.2.

For any point $q\in B_{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}(X,M)$ , there is a unique point on the length minimizing geodesic of $X$ from $\pi_{X,M}(q)$ to $\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(q)$ , such that the point is precisely of $\mathbf{d}_{X}$ distance

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{\mathbf{d}_{M}(q,\pi_{X,M}(q))}{\mathbf{d}_{X}\big(\pi_{X,M}(q),\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(q)\big)}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{c}}\mathbf{d}_{X}\big(\pi_{X,M}(q),\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(q)\big) $$

away from $\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(q)$ . Define

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{X,L}(q) $$

to be this unique point.

Here $\mathbf{g}_{c}$ is defined in Definition 7.1.1. By Facts 7.5.1, 7.5.2 and 7.5.4, the geometric significance of $\pi_{X,L}$ is that in the double Fermi coordinates, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{X,L}(l,x,z)=\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg). $$

The reader should consult Figure 6 and (7.1) for intuition.

*Figure 6. A schematic illustration of $\Pi_{X,L},\Pi_{Y,L}$*

#### 7.7.1. Calculating ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}$

With the coordinate expression (7.25) of $\Pi_{X,L}$ in double Fermi coordinate charts, we can calculate the differential ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}.$

At any point

$$ q=(l,x,z) $$

in our double Fermi coordinate chart centered at $p,$ use $\nu^{x}$ to denote any vector in $\mathbf{T}_{q}M$ with only nonzero components among $x_{1},\dots,x_{c}$ axes directions and

$$ \nu^{x}\perp_{|\cdot|}\partial_{x}. $$

We can then extend $\nu^{x}$ to a smooth vector field on our double Fermi coordinate chart by keeping all coefficients constant. In other words, for $\nu^{x}=\sum_{j}a^{j}\partial_{x_{j}}$ at $q=(l,x,z)$ , we define $\nu^{x}=\sum_{j}a^{j}\partial_{x_{j}}$ everywhere.

Similarly, use ${\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}$ to denote a vector in $\mathbf{T}_{q}M$ with only nonzero components among $z_{1},\dots,z_{c}$ axes directions and

$$ {\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}\perp_{|\cdot|}\partial_{z}. $$

Then extend ${\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}$ constantly in our double Fermi coordinate chart. By abusing the notations, we can calculate with Definition 7.1.1 in mind,

#### Lemma 7.7.3.

At point $q=(l,x,z)$ , if $\frac{|z|}{|x|}>t_{c}$ (defined 7.9), we have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v,w,u)=(v,0,0), $$

and if $\frac{|z|}{|x|}<t_{c}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v,0,0)= \displaystyle(v,0,0), \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,\partial_{x},0)= \displaystyle\bigg(0,\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x},0\bigg), \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,\nu^{x},0)= \displaystyle\bigg(0,\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{c}}\nu^{x},0\bigg), \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,0,\partial_{z})= \displaystyle\bigg(0,\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x},0\bigg), \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,0,{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z})= \displaystyle(0,0,0), $$

where the right hand sides always lie in $\mathbf{T}_{\Pi_{X,L}(q)}M.$ Moreover the kernel subspace $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}$ is spanned by

$$ \displaystyle-\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}+\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{z}, $$

and all ${\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}$ with only nonzero components among $z$ axes directions such that

$$ {\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}\perp_{|\cdot|}\partial_{z}. $$

#### Proof.

By definition, $\nu^{x}(|x|)=\nu^{x}(|z|)={\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}(|z|)={\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{z}(|x|)=0,$ so only ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,\partial_{x},0)$ and ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,0,\partial_{z})$ need our attention.

On the other hand, we have $\partial_{x}|x|=1,\frac{x}{|x|}=\partial_{x}$ and $\partial_{z}|z|=1,\frac{z}{|z|}=\partial_{z}.$ Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,\partial_{x},0)= \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{c}\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\prime}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg(-\frac{|z|}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)x \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg(\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)-\frac{1}{c}\frac{|z|}{|x|}\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\prime}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg)\partial_{x} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}. $$

We also have

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(0,0,\partial_{z})= \displaystyle\frac{1}{c}\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\prime}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg(\frac{1}{|x|}\bigg)x \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg(\frac{1}{c}\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\prime}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg)\partial_{x} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}-1}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}. $$

Then (7.26) is apparently mapped to $0$ by ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}.$ We are done. ∎

by replacing $X$ with $Y$ in Definition 7.7.1 and define

### 7.8. Intersection angles and wedge bundles

As mentioned when introducing Lawlor’s ideas, in the end we have to verify that the wedges $W_{(\theta,{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})}(X,L)$ and $W_{(\theta,{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}})}(Y,L)$ in the last subsection intersect only at $L$ . Testing how wedges intersect is a bit tricky. To this end, we need an angle condition and an auxiliary wedge bundle.

#### Fact 7.8.1.

For every point $p\in L,$ a tangent vector $v$ in $\mathbf{T}_{p}M$ can be uniquely written as a sum of orthogonal vectors:

$$ \displaystyle v=v_{L}+v_{L,X}+v_{X,M}, $$

where $v_{L}\in\mathbf{T}_{p}L,v_{L,X}\in\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,X),v_{X,M}\in\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(X,M)$ .

#### Definition 7.8.2.

Recall Assumption 7.4.4 and Fact 7.8.1, we will define the intersection angles $\Theta(X,Y)$ between $X$ and $Y$ . Geometrically speaking, $\Theta(X,Y)$ is the minimum possible angle between vectors in $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,X)$ and $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,Y)$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(X,Y)=\inf_{p}\inf_{v\in\mathbf{T}^{\perp}_{p}(L,Y)}\arctan\frac{\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert v_{L,X}\right\rVert}. $$

The tangent space to a submanifold captures the infinitesimal behavior of the submanifold. Along the same line, we need to capture the the infinitesimal structures of wedge neighborhoods in Definition 7.7.1, $W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)$ . To this end, we define a wedge bundle $W_{(\theta,\rho)}^{\mathbf{T}}(X,L)$ associated with the wedge neighborhood $W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)$ . Geometrically speaking, it just consists of all tangent vectors in $\mathbf{T}^{\perp}(L,M)$ that lie in the wedge neighborhood $W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)$ :

#### Definition 7.8.3.

Define the angle $\theta$ radius $\rho$ wedge bundle of $X$ with vertex $L$ to be

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\theta,\rho)}^{\mathbf{T}}(X,L)=\bigg\{(p,v)\in\mathbf{T}M\,|\,p\in L,v\in\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,M),\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert\leq\rho,\frac{\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert v_{L,X}\right\rVert}\leq\tan\theta\bigg\}. $$

Note that for the definition of wedge bundles $W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L),$ we no longer need $\rho\leq{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}},$ and even $\rho=\infty$ can be allowed. Similarly one can define

$$ W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(Y,L) $$

with every $X$ replaced by $Y$ in Fact 7.8.1 and Definition 7.8.3 . A very nice thing about the wedge bundles is that it is always easy to determine the intersection set of two wedge bundles $W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)$ and $W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(Y,L)$ , since one just has to do the algebraic problem in a vector bundle. We have the following fact.

#### Lemma 7.8.4.

With Assumption 7.4.4 in mind, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Theta(X,Y)=\Theta(Y,X). $$

Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)\cap W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(Y,L)=L, $$

provided

$$ \displaystyle\theta<\min\left\{\frac{\Theta(X,Y)}{2},\frac{\pi}{4}\right\}. $$

#### Proof.

Let us first prove that $\Theta(X,Y)=\Theta(Y,X).$

For any point $p\in L,$ let $S_{1}^{2c-1}(p)$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,M).$ Then $\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,X)$ and $\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,Y)$ intersect $S_{1}^{2c-1}$ at two great circle (i.e. totally geodesic) spheres $S_{X}^{c-1}$ and $S_{Y}^{c-1}$ , respectively, of dimension $c-1$ .

Now let $v$ denote a unit vector in $S_{Y}^{c-1}.$ Since $S_{X}^{c-1}$ is totally geodesic, elementary spherical geometry shows that

$$ \displaystyle\arctan\frac{\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert v_{L,X}\right\rVert}=\mathbf{d}_{S_{1}^{2c-1}(p)}(v,S_{X}^{c-1}). $$

Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\inf_{v\in\mathbf{T}^{\perp}_{p}(L,Y)}\arctan\frac{\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert v_{L,X}\right\rVert} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\inf_{v\in S_{Y}^{c-1}}\inf_{w\in S_{X}^{c-1}}\mathbf{d}_{S_{1}^{2c-1}(p)}(v,w) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\inf_{w\in S_{X}^{c-1}}\inf_{v\in S_{Y}^{c-1}}\mathbf{d}_{S_{1}^{2c-1}(p)}(v,w) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\inf_{w\in\mathbf{T}^{\perp}_{p}(L,X)}\arctan\frac{\left\lVert v_{Y,M}\right\rVert}{\left\lVert v_{L,Y}\right\rVert}. $$

Since $p$ is arbitrary, this implies that $\Theta(X,Y)=\Theta(Y,X).$

Using interpretation (7.28), it is easy to show that when restricted to a point $p$ , the two infinite radius wedge bundles

$$ \displaystyle W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(X,L),W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(Y,L) $$

are the cones over the closed domains

$$ \displaystyle B_{\theta}(S_{X}^{c-1},S^{2c-1}_{1}(p))=\{v\in S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)|\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(v,S_{X}^{c-1})\leq\theta\}, \displaystyle B_{\theta}(S_{Y}^{c-1},S^{2c-1}_{1}(p))=\{v\in S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)|\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(v,S_{Y}^{c-1})\leq\theta\}, $$

respectively. Thus, if $z\in W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(X,L)\cap W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(Y,L)$ at $p,$ then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{-1}z,S_{X}^{c-1})\leq\theta, \displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{-1}z,S_{Y}^{c-1})\leq\theta. $$

By the triangle inequality for distance, this implies that there are points $a\in S_{X}^{c-1}$ , and $b\in S_{Y}^{c-1}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(a,b)\leq\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(a,\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{-1}z)+\mathbf{d}_{S^{2c-1}_{1}(p)}(\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{-1}z,b)\leq 2\theta. $$

This is a contradiction to the fact that

$$ \inf_{w\in S_{X}^{c-1}}\inf_{v\in S_{Y}^{c-1}}\mathbf{d}_{S_{1}^{2c-1}(p)}(v,w)\geq\Theta(X,Y)>2\theta. $$

Thus, restricted to the point $p,$ we must have $W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(X,L)\cap W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(Y,L)=p.$ Since $p$ is arbitrary in $L$ , we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle L\subset W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)\cap W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}(Y,L)\subset W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(X,L)\cap W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\infty)}(Y,L)=L. $$

We are done. ∎

With Lemma 7.8.4 at hand, a natural idea is to use wedge bundles to help us determine how wedge neighborhoods intersect.

However, if a submanifold is not totally geodesic, then exponentiating its tangent bundle in the ambient manifold will not give us the submanifold. Similarly, in general

$$ \displaystyle\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}(W^{\mathbf{T}}_{(\theta,\rho)}({X,L}))\not=W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L). $$

Thus we need the following fact, which says that up to a negligible error, the wedge neighborhoods are contained in the exponentiated image of wedge bundles:

#### Fact 7.8.5.

With Assumption 7.4.4 in mind, we have

$$ \displaystyle W_{(\theta,\rho)}(X,L)\subset\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}\Big(W^{\mathbf{T}}_{\big(\big(1+O({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}+\rho)\big)\theta,\big(1+O({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}+\rho)\big)\rho\big)}(X,L)\Big), $$

where the term $O(\cdot)$ depends geometrically on $X,L,M,$ and the ambient metric.

#### Proof.

The proof is a direct calculation in the double Fermi coordinate adapted to $(L,X,M).$ At a point $p,$ let $v\in\mathbf{T}_{p}^{\perp}(L,M).$ Taylor’s theorem with remainders gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{M}(\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}v,\pi_{X,M}(\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}v))= \displaystyle(1+O({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}+\rho))\left\lVert v_{X,M}\right\rVert, \displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{X}(\pi_{X,M}(\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}v),\pi_{L,X}\circ\pi_{X,M}(\exp^{\perp}_{L,M}v))= \displaystyle(1+O({{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}+\rho))\left\lVert v_{L,X}\right\rVert, $$

and thus

### 7.9. Proving $\Pi_{X,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing

Now with the basic definitions and facts in hand, we are ready to achieve Step (4). Recall Assumption 7.6.3 and adopt a double Fermi coordinate chart of radius $(\rho,\rho,\rho)$ centered at $p\in\mathbf{F}$ .

Our goal in this section is to prove that the retraction $\Pi_{X,L}$ defined in Definition 7.7.2 on the minimal submanifold $X$ obtained in Lemma 7.4.3 is $d$ -area-non-increasing as defined in Definition 7.0.5 with respect to any ambient metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ , with $\Omega_{h}$ defined in Lemma 7.4.3.

The set $\{\frac{|z|}{|x|}=t_{c}\}$ is where $\Pi_{X,L}$ is not continuously differentiable and thus irrelevant to discussing the area-non-increasing property.

Thus, we only have to focus on the points of $q=(l,x,z)$ with

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|z|}{|x|}<t_{c}. $$

Then the kernel $\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}$ has dimension precisely $c$ . $$ \displaystyle{\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}\oplus{\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}. $$

Thus, to verify $\Pi_{X,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing, it suffices to show that ${\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}$ maps ${\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}$ to a $d$ -vector of length less than $1.$ In other words we want to show that

#### Claim 7.9.1.

And the above claim follows from

#### Claim 7.9.2.

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1})\wedge\dots\wedge{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}}\leq 1, $$

#### 7.9.1. The ideas of the calculations

The proof reduces to careful calculations in double Fermi coordinate charts defined in Definition 7.5.3. However, before delving into the detailed calculations, it is worthwhile to give a quick illustration of why the calculation works.

The basis we plan to use is obtained as follows. By Lemma 7.7.3, we already have a complementary subspace $W$ to ${\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}$ . The complementary subspace $W$ is spanned by the following vectors $w_{1},\dots,w_{d}.$

For $1\leq j\leq d-c$ , we set

$$ w_{j}=\partial_{l_{j}}. $$

From ${d-c+1}\leq j\leq{d-1},$ we let $w_{j}\in\mathbf{T}_{q}M$ be $c-1$ different orthonormal vectors in $|\cdot|$ in the $x$ -directions that spans the orthogonal complement of $\partial_{x}$ in $|\cdot|.$ In the notation of Lemma 7.7.3, $w_{d-c+1},\dots,w_{d-1}$ spans the space of $\nu^{x}$ vectors. Finally we let

$$ \displaystyle w_{d}=\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{z}. $$

We emphasize that the coordinate quadratic norm $|\cdot|$ in general does not agree with the ambient metric $g$ . Thus, the complementary space $W$ to ${\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}$ is not orthogonal to ${\ker{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}$ . Instead, our basis $v_{1},\dots,v_{d}$ will be defined as the images of the orthogonal projections of $w_{1},\dots,w_{d}$ on to ${\ker^{\perp}{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}}$ .

Our calculation proceeds in five steps, where each term $O(\cdot)$ depends geometrically on $L,X,M$ and the ambient metric:

- (1) First we show that $\displaystyle\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2}(1+O(|z|^{2})).$

- (2) Next we show that $\displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2}=(1+O(|z|^{2}))\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\sqrt{\det(l,x)}(l,x,0).$ Here $\sqrt{\det(l,x)}$ is the coefficient of the volume form of $X$ in the double Fermi coordinate chart, i.e,

$$ \operatorname{dvol}_{X}=\sqrt{\det(l,x)}dl_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dl_{d-c}\wedge dx_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx_{c}. $$

The symbol $\sqrt{\det(l,x)}(l,x,0)$ means evaluating this coefficient at $(l,x,0).$ Precisely at this step we use the fact that the mean curvature of $X$ is $0,$ i.e., $X$ being a minimal submanifold.

- (3) Next, we show that $\displaystyle\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}=\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)^{2}\sqrt{\det(l,x)}\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg)$

- (5) Finally, using all of the above steps, and $O(|z|^{2})=|x|^{2}O\big(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}\big)$ , we deduce from (7.13) that $\displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}}$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle\bigg(1+|x|O\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)$ $\displaystyle\leq$ $\displaystyle\bigg(1+O(|x|)\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\bigg(1-16\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle 1-\bigg(\frac{1}{16}+O(|x|)\bigg)\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}.$ After some basic preparational work, our calculation will be carried out in the order of the above five steps.

$$ \displaystyle g(v_{d},v_{d}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g\bigg(w_{d}+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}\bigg){\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z}+\sum_{1\leq j\leq c-1}O(|z|){\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}^{z},w_{d}+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}\bigg){\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z}+\sum_{1\leq j\leq c-1}O(|z|){\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}^{z}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(w_{d},w_{d})+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}\bigg)g(w_{d},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z})+O(|z|)\sum_{1\leq j\leq c-1}g(w_{d},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}^{z}) \displaystyle+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{4}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)g({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z})+O(|z|^{2})\sum_{1\leq i,j\leq c-1}g({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{i}^{z},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}^{z})+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{3}}{|x|}\bigg)\sum_{1\leq j\leq c-1}g({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{j}^{z},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{0}^{z}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(w_{d},w_{d})+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{4}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)+O(|z|^{2})+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{4}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)+O(|z|^{2})+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{4}}{|x|}\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(w_{d},w_{d})+O(|z|^{2}). $$

Similar calculations shows that for any $1\leq m,n\leq d,$ we always have

$$ \displaystyle g(v_{m},v_{n})=g(w_{m},w_{n})+O(|z|^{2}). $$

Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\det([g(v_{m},v_{n})]) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\det\big([g(w_{m},w_{n})+O(|z|^{2})]\big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\det([g(w_{m},w_{n})])\det(I_{d}+O(|z|^{2})) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+O(|z|^{2}))\det([g(w_{m},w_{n})]). $$

#### 7.9.6. Calculating $\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2}$

Let us first calculate $\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2}=\det([g(w_{m},w_{n})])$ .

Since $\partial_{z}$ is always perpendicular to $w_{1},\dots,w_{d-1},\partial_{x}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g\bigg(w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{z}\bigg),w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{x}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\partial_{z}\bigg)\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{z}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

At our point $q=(l,x,z)$ , recall the definition of $\nu_{j}^{x}$ , i.e, (7.29) and (7.30). Since $\nu_{j}^{x}$ are of constant value throughout our coordinate chart and $\partial_{x}$ is the radial vector field in the $x$ coordinate, at any point $(l^{\prime},ax,y^{\prime})$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{1}^{x}\wedge\dots\wedge\nu_{c-1}^{x}\wedge\partial_{x}=\pm\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}. $$

This implies that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

On the other hand, since $\partial_{z}\perp w_{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq d-1$ and $\left\lVert\partial_{z}\right\rVert=1,$ using determinant of block matrix, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{z}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

Now we want to compare $\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\right\rVert^{2}$ with $\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}.$

By the Laplace expansion of determinants, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\right\rVert^{2}+(-1)^{1+d}g(w_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1})g(w_{1},\partial_{x}) \displaystyle+\dots+(-1)^{d-1+d}g(w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-2}\wedge\partial_{x},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1})g(w_{d-1},\partial_{x}). $$

Using the Laplace expansion again, we have

$$ \displaystyle g(w_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1})g(w_{1},\partial_{x}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(-1)^{d-1+1}g(w_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1},w_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1})g(\partial_{x},w_{1})g(w_{1},\partial_{x}) \displaystyle+\dots+(-1)^{d-1+d-1}g(w_{2}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-2})g(\partial_{x},w_{d-1})g(w_{1},\partial_{x}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle O(|z|^{2}). $$

Similar calculation shows that

$$ \displaystyle g(w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge\overline{w_{j}}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x},w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1})g(w_{j},\partial_{x})=O(|z|^{2}), $$

where $\overline{w_{j}}$ means omitting the term $w_{j}.$

Thus, we can conclude

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\right\rVert^{2}+O(|z|^{2}). $$

In other words

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\right\rVert^{2}=\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{-2}\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d-1}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}+O(|z|^{2}). $$

Now, combine (7.47), (7.46), (7.45) into (7.43), and using $\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}=1+O(|z|)$ and (7.13), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert w_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge w_{d}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\big(\left\lVert\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{-2}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}+O(|z|^{2})\big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)O(|z|)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(1+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{3}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg)\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

Now bring (7.53) into (7.39), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(1+O\bigg(|z|^{2}+\frac{|z|^{3}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg)\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg) \displaystyle\cdot\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,z). $$

Here the last $(l,x,z)$ is to signify that $\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}$ is evaluated at $(l,x,z)$ .

#### 7.9.7. Calculating $\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}$

By Fact 7.9.5, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)^{2}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\nu_{1}^{x}\wedge\dots\wedge\nu_{c-1}^{x}\wedge\partial_{x}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

By (7.44), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert{\operatorname{d}}\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)^{2}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg). $$

Here the last $\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg)$ is to signify that we evaluate $\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}$ at $\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg)$ .

#### 7.9.8. $(l,x)$ volume element

At this stage, from (7.56) and (7.58) it is clear that in order to prove $\Pi_{X,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing, the key is to estimate

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}. $$

#### Definition 7.9.9.

We call the above expression (7.59) the $(l,x)$ volume elements.

We use the name $(l,x)$ volume element because the volume form of the $d$ -dimensional submanifolds $\{z=a\}$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}^{c}$ is precisely

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{dvol}_{\{z=a\}}=\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert dl_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dl_{d-c}\wedge dx_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge dx_{c}. $$

Estimating the $(l,x)$ volume element involves two steps.

First, let us prove that

#### Claim 7.9.10.

We have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,z)=(1+O(|z|^{2}))\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,0). $$

The above claim is the only place in this section that uses the fact of $X$ being a minimal submanifold.

#### Proof.

Again, we want to use Taylor’s theorem with remainders. To simplify our notation, set

$$ \displaystyle u_{1}=\partial_{l_{1}},\dots,u_{d-c}=\partial_{l_{d-c}}, \displaystyle u_{d-c+1}=\partial_{x_{1}},\dots,u_{d}=\partial_{x_{c}}. $$

At $(l,x,0)$ , using formulas for derivatives of determinants, we can calculate

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{z_{k}}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}\cdot\textnormal{tr}\big([g(u_{m},u_{n})]^{-1}[\partial_{z_{k}}g(u_{m^{\prime}},u_{n^{\prime}})]\big). $$

Here $[g(u_{m},u_{n})]$ means the matrix with the $mn$ -th entry being $g(u_{m},u_{n})$ and $[g(u_{m},u_{n})]^{-1}$ is the inverse matrix of $[g(u_{m},u_{n})]$ .

We have

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{z_{k}}g(u_{m},u_{n}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(\nabla_{\partial_{z_{k}}}u_{m},u_{n})+g(u_{m},\nabla_{\partial_{z_{k}}}u_{n}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle g(\nabla_{u_{m}}{\partial_{z_{k}}},u_{n})+g(u_{m},\nabla_{u_{n}}{\partial_{z_{k}}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle u_{m}\big(g({\partial_{z_{k}}},u_{n})\big)-g({\partial_{z_{k}}},\nabla_{u_{m}}u_{n})+u_{n}\big(g(u_{m},{\partial_{z_{k}}})\big)-u_{n}g(\nabla_{u_{n}}u_{m},{\partial_{z_{k}}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2g(\mathbf{A}_{X}(u_{m},u_{n}),\partial_{z_{k}}), $$

where $\mathbf{A}_{X}$ is the second fundamental form tensor of $X$ inside $M$ . At (7.65), we have used the fact that coordinate vector fields have zero lie bracket, so $0=[\partial_{z_{k}},u_{m}]=\nabla_{\partial_{z_{k}}}u_{m}-\nabla_{u_{m}}\partial_{z_{k}}$ , etc. At (7.67), we have used the fact that $\partial_{z_{k}}$ is always orthogonal to $u_{j}$ on $X.$

Thus, from (7.67), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\textnormal{tr}\big([g(u_{m},u_{n})]^{-1}[\partial_{z_{k}}g(u_{m^{\prime}},u_{n^{\prime}})] \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2\textnormal{tr}\bigg([g(u_{m},u_{n})]^{-1}[g(\mathbf{A}_{X}(u_{m^{\prime}},u_{n^{\prime}}),\partial_{z_{k}})]\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2g(\textnormal{tr}_{X}\mathbf{A}_{X}(\cdot,\cdot),\partial_{z_{k}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2g(\mathbf{H}_{X},\partial_{z_{k}}), $$

where $\textnormal{tr}_{X}$ means the Riemannian trace of the tensor $\mathbf{A}_{X}$ with respect to the metric on $X$ and $\mathbf{H}_{X}$ is the mean curvature of $X$ inside $M.$

Since $X$ is a minimal submanifold, the mean curvature of $X$ vanishes, i.e., $\mathbf{H}_{X}=0.$ Thus, bringing (7.71) to (7.62), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{z_{k}}\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}=0. $$

Since $l,x$ and $k$ are arbitrary, we deduce that on $X$ all the first derivatives of

$$ \left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2} $$

along $z$ -directions vanish. Thus, applying Taylor’s theorem with remainders, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,z)=\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,0)+O(|z|^{2}). $$

Since $\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}$ is bounded below geometrically from $0$ , we are done. ∎

Next we shall prove that

#### Claim 7.9.11.

We have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}\bigg(l,\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)x,0\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(1+O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,0). $$

#### Proof.

Define

$$ \displaystyle F(\tau)=\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}\bigg(l,\tau\frac{x}{|x|},0\bigg), $$

where here $\frac{x}{|x|}$ uses the $x$ in $q=(l,x,z).$ Then we have $F^{\prime}=O(1)$ . Thus,

$$ \displaystyle F(|x|)-F\bigg(\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)|x|\bigg)=O\bigg(1-\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\bigg)|x|. $$

By the factorization,

$$ \displaystyle 1-\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)=\frac{1-\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)}{\sum_{j=0}^{c-1}\mathbf{g}^{\frac{j}{c}}\left(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\right)}, $$

from Definition 7.1.1, we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle 1-\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)\leq 1-\mathbf{g}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)=\frac{2c^{2}-9}{8}\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}. $$

This implies that

$$ \displaystyle F(|x|)-F\bigg(\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\frac{1}{c}}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)|x|\bigg)=O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}\bigg). $$

We are done. ∎

#### 7.9.9. Wrapping up the proof

Combining (7.56) (7.58) (7.60) (7.73), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\frac{\bigg(1+O(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|})\bigg)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,0)}{(1+O(|z|^{2}))\bigg(1+O\bigg(|z|^{2}+\frac{|z|^{3}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg)\left\lVert\partial_{l_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{l_{d-c}}\wedge\partial_{x_{1}}\wedge\dots\wedge\partial_{x_{c}}\right\rVert^{2}(l,x,0)} \displaystyle=\bigg(\mathbf{c}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}+\mathbf{s}_{c}\bigg(\frac{|z|}{|x|}\bigg)^{2}\bigg)\bigg(1+O\bigg(|z|^{2}+\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|}+\frac{|z|^{3}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg). $$

By (7.13), we deduce that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}}\leq\bigg(1-\frac{1}{16}\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg)\bigg(1+(|x|^{2}+|x|+|z|)O\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg)\bigg) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 1-\bigg(\frac{1}{16}+O(|x|)\bigg)\bigg(\frac{|z|^{2}}{|x|^{2}}\bigg). $$

Thus, if $O(|x|)$ is small enough, then we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}}\leq 1, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert\Pi_{X,L}(v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d})\right\rVert^{2}}{\left\lVert v_{1}\wedge\dots\wedge v_{d}\right\rVert^{2}}=1\iff|z|=0. $$

This smallness of $O(|x|)$ can be achieved as follows.

In our setting, when $2[\Sigma]\not=0,$ by making ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ small in Lemma 7.4.3, $X$ can be made arbitrarily close to

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{-1}({B_{\eta}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}}\times S^{d-c}) $$

geometrically. By the bullet in Lemma 6.0.1, our base metric $h$ restricts to the standard product metric on

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{-1}(B_{\eta}^{2c}\times S^{d-c}). $$

This implies that

$$ \displaystyle\Pi_{B_{\eta}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}\times S^{d-c},\{0\}^{2c}\times S^{d-c}}(u,v)=\left(\Pi_{\mathbb{R}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c},\{0\}^{2c}}(u),\pi_{S^{d-c}}(v)\right), $$

for $(u,v)\in\left(B_{\eta}^{c}\times\{0\}^{c}\right)\times S^{d-c}$ , where $\pi_{S^{d-c}}$ denotes the projection on to the factor $S^{d-c}$ in $\Gamma^{-1}(B_{\eta}^{2c}\times S^{d-c}).$

Now if we run our calculations again in $h,$ then all contributions from curvatures disappear due to the splitting (7.80), and it is very quick to arrive that in our base metric $h$ , we have term $O(\cdot)$ in (7.75) equal to $0.$ Since the term $O(\cdot)$ in (7.75) depends geometrically on $L,X,M$ and the ambient metric, we deduce that as long as we set the ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ in Lemma 7.4.3 small enough, we have $|O(|x|)|<\frac{1}{32}$ in (7.75). When $2[\Sigma]=0,$ we add a $\pm$ sign to the (7.78), (7.79) and (7.80), meaning positively or negatively oriented. However, the argument goes through unchanged, so we can still deduce that $|O(|x|)|<\frac{1}{32}$ in (7.75).

Our choice of point $q=(l,x,z)$ with $\frac{|z|}{|x|}<t_{c}$ is arbitrary, so the estimates (7.76) and (7.77) holds for all $q=(l,x,z)$ with $\frac{|z|}{|x|}<t_{c}$ . Now recall our Assumption 7.6.3. Our choice of base point $p$ in the finite set $F$ is also arbitrary. Setting

$$ \eta=\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}, $$

we deduce that $\Pi_{X,L}$ is a $d$ -area-non-increasing as claimed. To sum it up, we have prove the following

#### Fact 7.9.12.

Recall Lemma 7.4.3. For any metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ , we have the following

- (1) In $U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),$ the retraction $\Pi_{X,L}$ in Definition 7.7.2 is defined everywhere,

- (2) $\Pi_{X,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing, wherever $\Pi_{X,L}$ is continuously differentiable and ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ in Lemma 7.4.3 is small enough,

- (3) $\Pi_{X,L}$ maps unit simple $d$ -vectors to unit simple $d$ -vectors only when restricted to $X.$

#### Remark 7.9.1.

Another way to achieve the smallness of $O(|x|)$ in (7.75) works in more general settings. We can first make the radius $\eta$ in $U_{\eta}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C))$ small in Lemma 7.4.3. This makes the maximum of $|x|$ small. Then make ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ small in Lemma 7.4.3, we can always achieve $|O(|x|)|<\frac{1}{32}$ by geometric dependence on $L,X,M$ and the ambient metric. However, this double parameter smallness argument is not needed for our case.

### 7.10. Proving that $\pi_{Y,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing

The same argument as in the previous subsection gives.

#### Fact 7.10.1.

Recall Lemma 7.4.3. For any metric $g\in\Omega_{h}$ , we have

- (1) In $U_{\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\rho}}_{\operatorname{product}}}}{4}}({\operatorname{Sing}}\,\sigma^{d-c}(C)),$ the retraction $\Pi_{Y,L}$ in Definition 7.27 is defined everywhere,

- (2) $\Pi_{Y,L}$ is $d$ -area-non-increasing, wherever $\Pi_{Y,L}$ is continuously differentiable and ${\epsilon_{\operatorname{sum}}}$ in Lemma 7.4.3 is small enough,
